metadata.version: English version of the guideline published in Japanese in 2023
metadata.summary: The guideline addresses the pathophysiology, classification, diagnosis, risk factors and treatment of meibomian gland dysfunction. It considers low-delivery and high-delivery forms, related ocular disorders, diagnostic assessments, and the effectiveness and safety of treatment options. Its recommendations are intended to support decisions by healthcare professionals and patients while leaving clinical decisions to the treating physician in consultation with the patient.

toxicities.incidence: 1 of 10 studies assessing adverse events reported an event; 9 reported none

associated_therapies: eyelid hygiene with a cleansing agent containing tea tree oil
eyelid hygiene with a conventional cleansing agent
toxicities.incidence: 21 of 40 eyes (52.5%) with a cleansing agent containing tea tree oil; 12 of 40 eyes (30%) with a conventional cleansing agent
prevention: Use caution because adverse events vary with the cleansing agent and were not serious in the cited study.

toxicities.event: Eye discomfort or dryness during eyelid hygiene
prevention: Use caution when selecting a cleansing agent; the reported events were not serious.

management.actions: Eye drops were discontinued in the affected case.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Eye drops were discontinued in 1 out of 14 cases (7.1%) after eye pain.

management.actions: The affected patients recovered immediately after discontinuation.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Oral administration was discontinued in the affected patients.

management.actions: The affected patients discontinued oral administration.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Oral administration was discontinued in the affected patients.

prevention: Exercise care when prescribing to patients with cardiovascular disorders.
Exercise caution with adverse events during the relatively long administration period of oral doxycycline.
Exercise caution with digestive symptoms reported during oral minocycline treatment.

toxicities.event: Pain, heat sensation, and partial eyelash loss
toxicities.incidence: Reported in 1 RCT; the events were described as infrequent
4 of 6 studies assessing adverse events reported mild events; 2 reported none

toxicities.event: Bleeding from the eyelid or meibomian gland orifices
recognition: Bleeding during probing from the eyelid or meibomian gland orifices

management.actions: None of the cited studies required a special intervention to stop bleeding.

toxicities.event: Invasiveness and burden of a prolonged examination
prevention: Consider these disadvantages when deciding whether to perform IVCM.

recognition: Severe discomfort associated with strong eyelid compression using a conformer or swab to obtain a large sample

infection_management.management: The guideline considers treatment of the associated meibomitis with antimicrobial agents essential. It describes systemic antimicrobial treatment responses in ocular surface inflammatory diseases in the same disease category.
The cited studies implicate Cutibacterium acnes in phlyctenular MRKC, particularly in young women; the guideline calls for antimicrobial treatment of the associated meibomitis.
The guideline describes presumed involvement, alongside Cutibacterium acnes, in non-phlyctenular MRKC and calls for antimicrobial treatment of the associated meibomitis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with MGD; the guideline does not assign these treatments to a formal sequence.
decision_rules: Use eyelid warming and eyelid hygiene as foundational care. Express accumulated meibum when appropriate.
Consider oral n-3 fatty acids, IPL therapy, or thermal pulsation therapy as treatment options, taking their availability and lack of JHI coverage into account.
Select treatment through clinician judgment and discussion with the patient; the guideline does not establish a sequence among these options.

recommended_regimens.name: Eyelid warming
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: A (strong): Strongly confident in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Strongly recommended for MGD. Warming devices are favored over a towel because studies reported less benefit with a towel.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Improvement in subjective symptoms and meibum grade was reported. Among the studies reviewed, subjective symptoms improved in 32 of 33 studies and meibum grade improved in 19 of 20 studies.

recommended_regimens.name: Eyelid hygiene
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effects
recommended_regimens.summary: Marginally recommended. Hygiene with water-moistened cotton balls may help symptoms and BUT; commercial cleansing agents may also improve eyelid and meibum findings. The agent used warrants attention because mild adverse events can occur.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In one RCT, eye irritation occurred in 21 of 40 eyes (52.5%) treated with a tea tree oil-containing cleansing agent and 12 of 40 eyes (30%) treated with a conventional cleansing agent.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral n-3 fatty acid administration
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Little confidence in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: May improve subjective symptoms, eyelid margin vascularity, and BUT. Suitable patients, dosage, formulation, and the contribution of the usual diet remain uncertain; products used for MGD are treated as supplements and are not covered by JHI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The reviewed RCTs used n-3 fatty acid supplementation of 1.0–3.3 g/day; this range is not presented as an established optimal dose.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The reviewed RCTs treated patients for 3 months in five studies and 1 year in another study.

recommended_regimens.name: IPL
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: A (strong): Strongly confident in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Improves symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and eyelid margin findings, meibum grade, BUT, and epithelial disorders. Despite the evidence-based case for strong implementation, the final recommendation is marginal because IPL was not approved for MGD in Japan as of November 2022 and lacks JHI coverage. An internationally standardized application protocol has not been established.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Among the reviewed studies, symptoms improved in four of five studies, meibum grade improved in five of five studies, and BUT improved in four of four studies assessing those outcomes. Reported adverse events were infrequent, mild, and reversible.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The reviewed RCTs used three, five, or eight applications, with schedules that varied by study; these are study protocols rather than a standardized regimen.

recommended_regimens.name: Thermal pulsation therapy
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: B (medium): Moderately confident in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for improving subjective symptoms and selected objective findings. The recommendation is marginal because JHI does not cover the procedure. Studies suggest that patients with milder changes in meibum quality and gland morphology and a shorter disease duration may benefit more, but these are not established eligibility requirements.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across eight RCTs of LipiFlow®, subjective symptoms improved in four studies, plugging in two out of four, meibum quality in three out of five, BUT in two out of seven, and corneal epithelial disorders in one out of five. No serious adverse events were reported.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The reviewed studies administered LipiFlow® once, for 12 minutes.

not_recommended.name: CsA eye drops
not_recommended.reason: The guideline marginally recommends against their use for MGD: reported benefits are limited, the evidence is very weak, and JHI does not cover this indication.

not_recommended.name: Ophthalmic ointments (excluding corticosteroid-based ophthalmic ointment)/oily eye drops
not_recommended.reason: No clear recommendation can be made because evidence for individual ointments and lipid-containing eye drops is insufficient; this is not a demonstrated absence of benefit.

response_assessment.method: Subjective symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT, epithelial disorders, and adverse events
response_assessment.interpretation: These are the guideline's principal treatment outcomes; it does not specify a common interim or end-of-treatment assessment time.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Some recommended treatments are not covered by JHI. The final choice remains with the attending physician in consultation with the patient, considering clinical findings, patient circumstances, facility resources, and insurance constraints.

decision_rules: Consider MGX to relieve accumulated meibum and improve symptoms; it may be combined with foundational eyelid care.
Do not routinely implement intraductal probing: its effect apart from accompanying treatments is uncertain, improvement in objective findings is limited, and the procedure is invasive.

recommended_regimens.name: MGX
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimated effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Marginally recommended for improving subjective symptoms in oMGD. Expression alone did not consistently improve meibum measures, BUT, Schirmer value, or corneal staining; compression-related pain is a patient burden.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reviewed studies of MGX alone found improvement in subjective symptoms without consistent improvement in objective findings.

not_recommended.name: Intraductal meibomian gland probing
not_recommended.reason: Marginally recommended against implementation. Although symptoms can improve, benefits for obstruction findings, meibum grade, BUT, and keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders are limited. The procedure is invasive, may need repetition, lacks JHI coverage, and its independent effect is uncertain.

response_assessment.method: Subjective symptoms, meibum quality and expressibility, BUT, and corneal epithelial findings
response_assessment.interpretation: Symptom improvement is the principal reported benefit of MGX; improvement in the objective measures is not consistently established for MGX alone.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No uniform MGX technique or treatment schedule is established in the reviewed studies. Bleeding from the eyelid or gland orifices may occur during probing; the reviewed studies did not report a need for special treatment to stop it.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with MGD; anti-inflammatory therapy is described when inflammatory findings are present, but the treatment recommendations listed here are not all restricted to that subgroup.
decision_rules: When inflammation is present, the guideline describes adding anti-inflammatory treatment with eye drops or oral medication to foundational eyelid care.
For antimicrobial eye drops, the supportive treatment evidence and marginal recommendation concern azithromycin eye drops rather than antimicrobial eye drops as a whole.
Consider JHI eligibility when MGD coexists with blepharitis or another covered ocular condition; coverage for MGD alone differs by treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Azithromycin eye drops
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: B (medium): Moderately confident in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Marginally recommended to improve symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, and meibum grade. Effects on BUT and epithelial disorders are more limited. Adverse events are relatively frequent but generally mild; JHI covers treatment when concomitant blepharitis is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical corticosteroids
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Corticosteroid eye drops, studied with eyelid warming and hygiene or with an antibiotic and hygiene, may improve symptoms and ocular findings. Evidence is limited; the reviewed treatment evidence did not establish efficacy of corticosteroid ointments for MGD. JHI coverage applies with concomitant blepharitis, not MGD alone.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In one RCT, adding 0.5% loteprednol etabonate to warming and hygiene produced significantly greater improvements in BUT, staining, eyelid margin findings, and meibum quality than warming and hygiene alone. This formulation could not be prescribed in Japan.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The cited RCT of 0.5% loteprednol etabonate treated patients for 2 months; this is a study duration, not a guideline-wide schedule.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral azithromycin
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: B (medium): Moderately confident in estimated effect
recommended_regimens.summary: Marginally recommended for improving symptoms and meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings. Its effect on meibum grade is unknown, and benefits for BUT and epithelial disorders are limited. It lacks JHI coverage for ocular disease; cardiovascular adverse effects require attention in patients with cardiovascular disorders.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral doxycycline
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Little confidence in estimated effect
recommended_regimens.summary: A marginally recommended oral tetracycline option for symptoms and meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings. Effects on meibum grade are unclear and BUT benefit is limited. Adverse events, particularly digestive symptoms, are relatively frequent, and JHI does not cover MGD.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral minocycline
recommended_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Little confidence in estimated effect
recommended_regimens.summary: A marginally recommended oral tetracycline option that is likely to improve symptoms and meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings. Its effect on meibum grade remains unclear; caution is required regarding adverse events. JHI does not cover MGD.

response_assessment.method: Subjective symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT, epithelial disorders, and adverse events
response_assessment.interpretation: The relative importance and demonstrated improvement of these outcomes differ by treatment.

supportive_care: Continue appropriate eyelid warming and hygiene when these are part of the selected treatment approach.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline cautions against oral antimicrobial administration in renal damage, liver damage, infants, children, and pregnancy; it additionally advises avoiding minocycline during breastfeeding. Tetracycline was discussed, but excluded from recommendation-strength and evidence-strength assessment because only one relevant article was available. No uniform drug dose or course for the recommended antimicrobials is specified.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with both MGD and dry eye.
decision_rules: Treat accompanying dry eye according to its type and severity while addressing MGD.
DQS eye drops may improve outcomes when MGD coexists with dry eye; the studies reviewed did not establish their efficacy for MGD without dry eye.
Do not interpret possible benefit in concurrent dry eye as a recommendation to use DQS eye drops for MGD alone.

alternative_regimens.name: DQS eye drops
alternative_regimens.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effect
alternative_regimens.summary: In studies restricted to patients with concurrent MGD and dry eye, DQS eye drops may improve symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT, and ocular surface epithelial damage. The guideline nevertheless marginally recommends against implementing DQS as a treatment for MGD because MGD alone is not covered by JHI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Concurrent dry eye; DQS use for dry eye is covered by JHI, whereas its efficacy and coverage as treatment for MGD alone are not established.

not_recommended.name: DQS eye drops for MGD alone
not_recommended.reason: Marginally recommend “not to be implemented”. Efficacy without concurrent dry eye is unknown, and JHI does not cover DQS for MGD alone.

response_assessment.method: Subjective symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT, and ocular surface epithelial damage
response_assessment.interpretation: Possible improvements with DQS were reported in patients who had both MGD and dry eye; they cannot be assumed for MGD without dry eye.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The DQS studies used differing schedules and observation periods; the guideline does not set a regimen for MGD. Reported adverse effects included eye pain, irritation, tearing, and discharge.

conditions.name: MGD
conditions.description: A group of conditions in which meibomian gland function is diffusely abnormal for various reasons and chronic ocular discomfort is present. The guideline classifies MGD into low-delivery and high-delivery types. Its relationship with tear evaporation is clinically important, although the precise contribution of the tear lipid layer to evaporation control in humans remains unsettled.
conditions.epidemiology: Japanese surveys estimate MGD prevalence at about 10–30% among people aged ≥50 years, although the exact prevalence is uncertain and varies with diagnostic criteria. In a Japanese population-based study of residents aged 6–96 years, age-group prevalence was 0% (6–19 years), 11.8% (20–29 years), 5.6% (30–39 years), 21.6% (40–49 years), 32.8% (50–59 years), 41.9% (60–69 years), 48.4% (70–79 years), and 63.9% (80–96 years). Reported associated factors include aging, male sex, menopause, androgen deficiency, Asian ethnicity, rural residence, VDT-related work, smoking, SCL use, glaucoma eye drops, ocular surgery, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, hyperthyroidism, rosacea, SS, SJS, and GVHD. Associations vary across studies.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reported symptoms include ocular discomfort, foreign body sensation, dryness, pressure, pain, burning, tearing, ocular fatigue, blurred vision, itching, discharge, and photophobia. No symptom has been established as distinguishing MGD from other ocular surface disorders. Findings can include altered meibum, obstruction of gland orifices, eyelid margin vascularity or irregularity, and MCJ displacement. Ocular surface epithelial abnormalities and dry eye may coexist.

subtypes.name: Low-delivery type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced delivery of meibum; the revised classification comprises congenital, obstructive, and atrophic categories.

subtypes.name: High-delivery type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An increased amount of qualitatively altered meibum is expressed, including with mild eyelid compression; its pathophysiology remains poorly understood.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify relevant subjective symptoms and distinguish symptoms attributable to other ocular surface disorders.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms contribute to the clinical assessment but do not, by themselves, specifically distinguish MGD.

diagnostic_workup.test: Slit-lamp microscopy of eyelid margins and meibum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess gland-orifice obstruction, surrounding eyelid changes, and the quantity, quality, and expressibility of meibum.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Plugging, pouting, capping, ridges, vascularity, MCJ displacement, and margin irregularity can support diagnosis. Meibum appearance and expressibility require interpretation alongside symptoms and other findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess meibomian gland morphology, including structural loss.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline recommends its diagnostic use, but device-dependent image differences and imperfect correspondence between morphology and ocular surface function require caution.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate tear-film stability and associated dry eye.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: BUT is often shorter in MGD, but it is not specific enough to diagnose MGD alone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the tear-film disruption pattern and associated dry-eye type.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No BUP specific to MGD has been established; evidence is insufficient to decide whether to recommend it for MGD diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure tear-film stability without fluorescein.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Studies conflict and there is no standardized MGD cut-off; it is not currently recommended as an MGD diagnostic test.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess keratoconjunctival epithelial abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline identifies it as the most versatile staining method for these abnormalities, not as an MGD-specific test.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess ocular surface epithelial abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It is an available staining method, without an established MGD-specific pattern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess conjunctival epithelial abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It is an available staining method, without an established MGD-specific pattern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate tear lipid-layer appearance and thickness.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A thinner LLT has been reported in MGD, but a validated cut-off is lacking and tear-volume-related factors affect interpretation; the diagnostic value of interference patterns remains unresolved.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess evaporation as a possible reflection of meibomian gland function.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Equipment and conditions lack standardization, so the guideline does not recommend it for MGD diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine tissue features at the cellular level.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reported diagnostic findings require caution because the identity of structures described as acini needs confirmation; contact, invasiveness, and examination burden also matter.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a possible consequence of altered tear-film function.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diagnostic studies conflict. The guideline does not discourage testing but considers its present clinical utility limited.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure lipids at the eyelid margin.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Despite relatively reproducible semi-quantitation, the absence of an established cut-off limits diagnostic benefit.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate secretion composition.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neither MGD-specific markers nor analysis methods have been established; it is not presently useful for clinical diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a potential supplementary diagnostic approach.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No sufficiently useful MGD-specific biomarker has been established for current diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: Bacteriological culture and genomic sequencing using polymerase chain reaction
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate ocular surface or meibum microorganisms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neither approach has produced findings characteristic of MGD and neither is currently useful for its diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: Schirmer test or phenol red thread test
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess tear secretion during broader evaluation of MGD and dry eye.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In the outpatient assessment sequence described from the TFOS report.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These assessments do not independently establish MGD.

definitions.description: Minimally altered secretion quality and expressibility, without symptoms or corneal staining.
Mild alteration of secretion quality and expressibility, minimal to mild symptoms, and no to limited corneal staining.
Moderate alteration of secretion quality and expressibility, moderate symptoms, and mild to moderate staining mainly at the periphery.
Severe alteration of secretion quality and expressibility, marked symptoms, and marked staining that also affects the center.

staging.additional_rules: The system also identifies “Plus” disease when ocular surface or eyelid disorders coexist or accompany MGD. This severity classification has not achieved worldwide standardization.

prognostic_tools.name: Meibum grade

risk_groups.criteria: Cloudy secretion expressed with light compression.
Cloudy secretion expressed with moderate compression.
Secretion cannot be expressed even with strong compression.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: This semi-quantitative measure is used to assess MGD severity and response to treatment.

prognostic_tools.name: OSDI
components: Subjective symptoms assessed with a 12-item questionnaire
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The TFOS staging table uses an OSDI grade of 0–100 alongside symptoms, gland changes, and meibum quality; it is not presented as a stand-alone MGD diagnostic criterion.

prognostic_tools.name: Meibum quality score
components: Quality scores from eight glands in the middle 1/3 of the lower eyelid
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Each gland receives 0–3; the summed score ranges from 0–24. If obstruction prevents expression from some glands, a summed quality score can decrease despite progression.

conditions.name: Low-delivery type
conditions.description: The reduced-delivery category of MGD. Ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization and acinar atrophy are its principal proposed pathological processes; acinar atrophy may arise primarily with aging or secondarily after obstruction. The revised classification separates congenital, obstructive, and atrophic forms.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline states that most Japanese MGD cases are low-delivery type. Possible secondary causes include ageing, allergic eye disease, blepharitis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, pemphigus oculus, graft-versus-host disease, Sjögren's syndrome, trachoma, drug-induced disorders, chemical wounds, and burns.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reduced meibum delivery may accompany orifice obstruction, decreased secretion on eyelid compression, and evaporative dry eye with dryness or ocular fatigue. Symptoms attributable to gland changes cannot reliably be separated from those attributable to associated tear-film and ocular surface changes.

subtypes.name: Congenital
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A separate category within the revised low-delivery classification; further defining clinical features are not specified.

subtypes.name: Obstructive
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diffuse orifice obstruction; the revised classification distinguishes primary and secondary forms.

subtypes.name: Atrophic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diffuse acinar atrophy; the revised classification distinguishes primary and secondary forms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the symptomatic component of the revised diagnostic criteria.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating suspected low-delivery type MGD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms clearly caused by another ocular surface disease must be excluded when deciding whether this criterion is met.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect diffuse obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating suspected low-delivery type MGD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diffuse obstruction satisfies criterion I within the eyelid-margin and secretion-abnormality component.

diagnostic_workup.test: Meibum expression after moderate eyelid compression by the thumb or compression with forceps or clamps
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess reduced expression or expression of viscous meibum.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating suspected low-delivery type MGD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced expression or viscous secretion satisfies criterion II. Diagnosis requires subjective symptoms together with either criterion I or criterion II; meeting both I and II supports the obstructive subtype.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of eyelid vascularity or redness, MCJ displacement, eyelid margin irregularity, meibography dropout, corneal abnormalities, BUT, and BUP
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional information for subtype diagnosis, severity assessment, and differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These findings can be useful but are not mandatory elements of the revised diagnostic criteria.

staging.additional_rules: The revised diagnostic criteria concern low-delivery type MGD only; a globally accepted severity system is not established.

conditions.name: Obstructive
conditions.description: A low-delivery subtype characterized by diffuse obstruction of meibomian gland orifices. Ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization and increased meibum viscosity can reduce drainage; obstruction can also precede secondary acinar atrophy. The revised classification distinguishes primary and secondary forms.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Orifices may show plugging, pouting, capping, or ridges. Meibum can become cloudy, yellow or white, granular, viscous, or toothpaste-like, and its expression can diminish. Ocular discomfort and associated dry-eye symptoms may occur; inflammatory findings are not necessarily apparent in early or mild disease.

subtypes.name: primary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification category within obstructive low-delivery MGD.

subtypes.name: secondary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A classification category in which an associated condition or exposure may contribute to low-delivery MGD.

diagnostic_workup.test: Slit-lamp microscopy of gland orifices and expressed meibum
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify obstruction and evaluate secretion quality and expressibility.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When obstructive low-delivery MGD is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Within the revised low-delivery criteria, concurrent diffuse orifice obstruction and reduced or viscous meibum expression support this subtype when the required subjective symptoms are also present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess gland structure and dropout as a supplementary finding.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When supporting diagnosis or characterizing the subtype.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Structural dropout can accompany disease but is not an essential component of the revised low-delivery diagnostic criteria.

conditions.name: Atrophic
conditions.description: A low-delivery subtype with diffuse acinar atrophy. Atrophy may follow pressure associated with retained material or arise from changes affecting glandular cells themselves; aging-related primary atrophy need not involve ductal hyperkeratinization. Primary and secondary forms are recognized.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Meibum expression is decreased. Atrophic acini have been described as small and irregular rather than rounded, and gland dropout may be visible on meibography.

subtypes.name: primary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An atrophic category that can arise through changes intrinsic to glandular cells.

subtypes.name: secondary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An atrophic category that can develop following gland obstruction or other contributing influences.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify diminished secretion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating suspected atrophic low-delivery MGD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced expression can satisfy criterion II of the revised low-delivery criteria even without diffuse orifice obstruction, provided the required subjective symptoms are present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess gland dropout as an additional subtype-related finding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Dropout supports assessment but is not mandatory for the revised diagnosis.

conditions.name: High-delivery type
conditions.description: An MGD category in which a large amount of qualitatively altered meibum is expressed. Its underlying pathophysiology is not well established, including whether secretion truly rises or appears increased after mild obstruction resolves. The revised guideline treats it as one category rather than assigning established subcategories.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline describes high-delivery MGD as relatively more common in Western countries than in Japan. It is often associated with seborrheic dermatitis, rosacea, or acne vulgaris.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Ocular symptoms and eyelid-margin changes can resemble those of low-delivery MGD, including vascularity, MCJ displacement, and margin irregularity, but eyelid compression expresses an increased quantity of lipid. Few structural abnormalities may be visible on meibography.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of subjective symptoms, eyelid margins, and meibum on compression
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize symptoms, orifice-area abnormalities, and increased lipid expression.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline does not establish diagnostic criteria for this category. A cited study reported diagnostic sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 96.7% when subjective symptoms were ≥ 2 and eyelid-margin abnormalities were ≥ 2; this is a study result, not an adopted diagnostic standard.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess gland morphology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited report observed few structural abnormalities in high-delivery MGD.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline provides no diagnostic criteria or established severity staging specific to high-delivery MGD.

conditions.name: Meibomitis
conditions.description: Inflammation involving the meibomian glands. In Japanese clinical usage described by the guideline, the term has historically referred particularly to gland inflammation associated with bacterial growth. It can accompany oMGD and ocular surface inflammatory lesions, but inflammation is not present in every case of MGD.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Inflammatory findings can include redness and swelling around obstructed gland orifices and the eyelid margin. Associated corneal findings may include epithelial abnormalities or phlycten.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical examination of gland orifices, eyelid margins, and ocular surface
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify gland-associated inflammation and any accompanying corneal or conjunctival involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When meibomitis or an associated ocular surface inflammatory disorder is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Inflammation helps characterize meibomitis but is not required to identify all MGD.

conditions.name: MRKC
conditions.description: An ocular surface inflammatory condition associated with meibomitis. The guideline distinguishes a phlyctenular form with corneal cellular infiltration from a non-phlyctenular form characterized predominantly by SPK. MRKC frequently coexists with oMGD.
conditions.epidemiology: The phlyctenular form is reported predominantly in young women. The non-phlyctenular form occurs in both young and older people.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Meibomitis involves retained meibum at gland orifices and redness and swelling near the orifices, eyelid margin, or palpebral conjunctiva. The phlyctenular form includes corneal cellular infiltration and superficial vascularization; the non-phlyctenular form mainly shows SPK without cellular infiltration. In older patients, SPK related to MRKC can be difficult to distinguish from SPK related to dry eye.

subtypes.name: phlyctenular type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Corneal cellular infiltration and superficial vascularization accompany meibomitis; the guideline reports an association with Cutibacterium acnes.

subtypes.name: non-phlyctenular type
subtypes.distinguishing_features: SPK predominates without cellular infiltration; involvement of Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus species is presumed.

diagnostic_workup.test: Examination of gland orifices, eyelid margin, palpebral conjunctiva, and cornea
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify meibomitis and distinguish the reported corneal patterns.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When ocular surface inflammation accompanies suspected meibomitis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Corneal infiltration with superficial vascularization favors the phlyctenular form; predominantly SPK without infiltration favors the non-phlyctenular form.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline reports that severity of both MRKC forms correlates with severity of meibomitis and ocular surface epithelial abnormalities, without supplying a separate staging scale.

conditions.name: Posterior blepharitis
conditions.description: Inflammation at the posterior eyelid margin, near the meibomian gland orifices. MGD can contribute to posterior blepharitis, but posterior blepharitis can also occur without MGD; the guideline does not treat the terms as interchangeable.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Inflammation affects the region posterior to the eyelid margin’s gray line. Meibomitis with obstructed orifices and a red, swollen surrounding area is presented as a typical example.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical examination of the posterior eyelid margin and meibomian gland orifices
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the location of inflammation and assess for coexisting MGD or meibomitis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Posterior-margin inflammation establishes the anatomical pattern; it does not by itself establish MGD.

therapies_index.name: eyelid warming
therapies_index.administration: Home treatment; the guideline favors warming devices over a towel. Treatment frequency and duration vary among the cited studies.
key_toxicities: A temporary, reversible adverse event was reported in one study, without further characterization.

therapies_index.name: MGDRx
therapies_index.administration: Used as an eyelid-warming device in a study of MGD.

therapies_index.name: Eyebag
therapies_index.administration: Used as an eyelid-warming device in a study of MGD.

therapies_index.name: Blephasteam
therapies_index.administration: Used as an eyelid-warming device in studies of MGD.

therapies_index.name: Eye mask
therapies_index.administration: Used for eyelid warming in a study of MGD.

therapies_index.name: Azuki no chikara
therapies_index.administration: Used as an eyelid-warming device in a study of MGD.

therapies_index.name: eyelid hygiene
therapies_index.administration: Studies wiped the eyelids with water-moistened cotton balls or commercially available cleansing agents; methods and frequency differed.
key_toxicities: Some cleansing agents caused non-serious eye irritation, discomfort, or dryness.

therapies_index.name: cotton balls moistened with water
therapies_index.administration: Used to wipe the eyelids in an observational study.

therapies_index.name: commercially available cleansing agents
therapies_index.administration: Applied to wipe the eyelids; study methods differed.
key_toxicities: Eye irritation, discomfort, and dryness may occur with certain agents; the reported events were not serious.

therapies_index.name: cleansing agent containing tea tree oil
therapies_index.administration: Used to clean one eye in a study comparing eyelid cleansing agents.
key_toxicities: The study reported eye irritation in 21 of 40 eyes (52.5%).

therapies_index.name: baby shampoo
therapies_index.administration: Used for eyelid hygiene in both groups of a CsA study.

therapies_index.name: MGX
therapies_index.administration: Studies expressed meibum with cotton swabs, tweezers, or forceps; schedules differed. MGX is not covered by JHI.
key_toxicities: Pain during gland compression can burden patients.

therapies_index.name: eyelid massage
therapies_index.administration: Used alongside eyelid warming and hygiene in both groups of a CsA study.

therapies_index.name: DQS eye drops
approved_indications: Dry eye under JHI; use for MGD alone is not approved.
therapies_index.administration: Studies in patients with both MGD and dry eye administered DQS six times a day for 3 months, four times a day for ≥4 months (4–16 months), or for 2 months; another compared a single drop with artificial tears.
key_toxicities: Eye pain led to discontinuation in 1 out of 14 cases (7.1%) in one study.
Eye irritation, tearing, and discharge occurred in 2 out of 32 cases (6.3%) in another study.

therapies_index.name: artificial tears
therapies_index.administration: Used as a comparator or concomitant treatment; one MGX study administered them four times a day.

therapies_index.name: azithromycin eye drops
therapies_index.mechanism: Azithromycin inhibits bacterial growth and eyelid bacterial lipase, has anti-inflammatory effects, and promotes lipid secretion from meibomian gland epithelial cells.
therapies_index.administration: Topical formulations in the reviewed studies ranged from 1.0% to 1.5%; dosing frequency and treatment duration varied. JHI covers use when blepharitis accompanies MGD.
key_toxicities: Adverse events were relatively frequent but generally mild.
Eye irritation and blurred vision were attributed to the eye drops' high viscosity.

therapies_index.name: ophthalmic ointments
therapies_index.administration: Topical ophthalmic use; the reviewed non-corticosteroid products included antimicrobial, immunosuppressant, and vitamin D3 ointments. The guideline could not make a clear recommendation for this category.

therapies_index.name: ofloxacin ophthalmic ointment
therapies_index.administration: Ophthalmic ointment; the guideline provides no dosing schedule.

therapies_index.name: vitamin D3
therapies_index.mechanism: Reported to suppress keratinization and inflammation.
therapies_index.administration: An ophthalmic ointment containing vitamin D3 was assessed for MGD; no dosing schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: immunosuppressant ointments
therapies_index.administration: Ophthalmic use; the ointments assessed are not covered by JHI for MGD.
key_toxicities: Burning sensation was reported.

therapies_index.name: lipid-containing eye drops
therapies_index.mechanism: Their lipid content can supplement the tear lipid component; products containing polar lipids were also reported to improve tear film stability.
therapies_index.administration: Topical ophthalmic use; ready-to-use products discussed in the guideline were sold overseas and lacked JHI coverage for MGD.
key_toxicities: Non-serious adverse events occurred in two of the five studies that assessed them.

therapies_index.name: castor oil
therapies_index.mechanism: The guideline describes anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects.
therapies_index.administration: Studied in lipid-containing eye drops; preparation and low-temperature storage were required.

therapies_index.name: perfluorohexyl octane
therapies_index.administration: A component of lipid-containing eye drops studied for MGD; no dosing schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: mineral oil
therapies_index.administration: A component of lipid-containing eye drops studied for MGD; no dosing schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: corticosteroid eye drops
approved_indications: Concomitant blepharitis under JHI; MGD alone is not covered.
therapies_index.administration: The reviewed studies combined topical corticosteroids with eyelid warming and hygiene, or combined corticosteroid and antibiotic eye drops with eyelid hygiene.

therapies_index.name: 0.5% loteprednol etabonate
therapies_index.administration: Lee et al. studied eye drops for 2 months alongside twice-daily eyelid warming and eyelid hygiene. The studied corticosteroid eye drops could not be prescribed in Japan.
key_toxicities: The cited study found no significant between-group difference in increased intraocular pressure and reported no serious adverse events.

therapies_index.name: betamethasone 0.1%-sulfacetamide sodium 10%
therapies_index.administration: Akyol-Salman et al. studied combined corticosteroid and antibiotic eye drops with eyelid hygiene for one month.
key_toxicities: The cited study reported no serious adverse events or increase in intraocular pressure.

therapies_index.name: betamethasone
therapies_index.administration: Present at 0.1% in combined eye drops studied with sulfacetamide sodium 10%.

therapies_index.name: sulfacetamide sodium
therapies_index.administration: Present at 10% in combined eye drops studied with betamethasone 0.1%.

therapies_index.name: N-acetyl-cysteine
therapies_index.administration: Eye drops were compared with betamethasone 0.1%-sulfacetamide sodium 10%; both groups also performed eyelid hygiene for one month.

therapies_index.name: CsA eye drops
therapies_index.mechanism: A cited study suggested that anti-inflammatory effects may reduce meibomian gland inflammation; the guideline characterizes any contribution to MGD improvement as limited or indirect.
therapies_index.administration: The studies used 0.05% eye drops. JHI does not cover their use for MGD, and the guideline marginally recommends against that use.

therapies_index.name: Restasis®
therapies_index.administration: Identified as a commercially available overseas CsA eye-drop product thought to have been used at 0.05% in the reviewed studies.

therapies_index.name: n-3 (omega-3) fatty acid administration
approved_indications: MGD, as a marginally recommended oral supplement; JHI does not cover its use for MGD.
therapies_index.administration: Oral supplementation was 1.0–3.3 g/day in the reviewed RCTs. Treatment lasted 3 months in five studies and 1 year in another; formulations differed.
key_toxicities: Digestive upset occurred in two out of 64 patients (3.12%) in one study and resolved after discontinuation.
Fish-tasting regurgitation led two out of 64 patients (3.12%) to discontinue treatment in another study.

therapies_index.name: EPA
therapies_index.administration: Included with DHA at differing ratios in oral n-3 fatty acid formulations studied for MGD.

therapies_index.name: DHA
therapies_index.administration: Included with EPA at differing ratios in oral n-3 fatty acid formulations studied for MGD.

therapies_index.name: DPA
therapies_index.administration: Included with vitamins A, C, and E in formulations used in two n-3 fatty acid studies.

therapies_index.name: ALA
therapies_index.administration: Included as the n-3 fatty acid in one study's oral formulation, alongside n-6 (linoleic acid) and n-9 (oleic acid).

therapies_index.name: azithromycin
therapies_index.mechanism: Acts bacteriostatically, inhibits bacterial lipase, has anti-inflammatory effects, and is reported to promote lipid secretion from meibomian gland epithelial cells.
therapies_index.administration: Oral use for MGD was marginally recommended but has no JHI coverage for ocular diseases; the guideline gives no oral dose or schedule.
key_toxicities: Oral-treatment adverse events were infrequent and judged mild in the cited studies.
Cardiovascular symptoms have been reported; the guideline calls for care when prescribing to patients with cardiovascular disorders.

therapies_index.name: doxycycline
therapies_index.mechanism: In addition to bacteriostatic activity, tetracycline-based antimicrobials inhibit bacterial lipases and suppress cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
therapies_index.administration: Oral treatment was marginally recommended for MGD, although JHI does not cover MGD. No recommended oral dose or schedule is specified.
key_toxicities: Adverse events with oral treatment were relatively frequent, particularly digestive symptoms.

therapies_index.name: minocycline
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as bacteriostatic, inhibitory to bacterial lipase in the eyelids, and anti-inflammatory.
approved_indications: Dacryocystitis and hordeolum under JHI; MGD is not covered.
therapies_index.administration: Oral treatment was marginally recommended for MGD. One combination-treatment study administered 100 mg twice a day; the guideline does not establish this as a recommended dose.
key_toxicities: Digestive symptoms occurred at low frequency in a cited RCT.
The guideline advises refraining from use in infants, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and patients with liver or kidney disease.

therapies_index.name: tetracycline
therapies_index.mechanism: Tetracycline-based antimicrobials are described as inhibiting bacterial growth and lipases and suppressing cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
therapies_index.administration: Oral use was examined, but the guideline excluded tetracycline from its assessments of recommendation strength and evidence strength because only one relevant article was available.

therapies_index.name: IPL
therapies_index.mechanism: Studies reported reduced tear inflammatory cytokines after treatment; liquefaction of meibum as deeper skin temperature rises was also proposed as a mechanism.
approved_indications: MGD in the United States, South Korea, China, and Taiwan; not approved for MGD in Japan as of November 2022.
therapies_index.administration: Reviewed RCTs treated the lower eyelids only, with three, five, or eight applications. Reported intervals were every 3 weeks, every 4 weeks, or days 1, 15, and 45. Some studies also performed meibum expression. Japan had no JHI coverage.
key_toxicities: Pain, heat sensation, and partial eyelash loss were reported in one RCT; the events were described as infrequent, mild, and reversible.
Long-term safety for ocular tissues including the lens and retina had not been confirmed.

therapies_index.name: thermal pulsation therapy
therapies_index.administration: The reviewed studies applied LipiFlow® once for 12 minutes. LipiFlow® was approved as a medical device in Japan in 2019 but was not covered by JHI as of 2021.
key_toxicities: Discomfort immediately after treatment was the principal adverse event in four studies; no serious events were reported.

therapies_index.name: LipiFlow®
therapies_index.administration: Applied once for 12 minutes in each of the reviewed thermal-pulsation studies; approved as a medical device in Japan in 2019, without JHI coverage as of 2021.
key_toxicities: Immediate post-treatment discomfort was reported; the cited studies reported no serious events.

therapies_index.name: intraductal meibomian gland probing
therapies_index.mechanism: A device is used to open obstructed meibomian gland orifices.
therapies_index.administration: Studied for oMGD, often alongside other treatments. The guideline marginally recommends against implementation because the procedure is invasive, may require repetition, and lacks JHI coverage.
key_toxicities: Bleeding from the eyelid or gland orifices may occur during probing; cited studies did not require special treatment to stop it.

therapies_index.name: 0.1% fluorometholone eye drops
therapies_index.administration: In one study, given three times a day in a combination treatment that included MGX. Another study compared use with and without probing.

therapies_index.name: 1.5% levofloxacin eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Given four times a day in an MGX study as part of treatment also including an eye mask, eyelid hygiene, other eye drops, and oral minocycline.

therapies_index.name: 0.1% hyaluronic acid eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Given four times a day in combination-treatment groups of MGX studies; another study used the drops for 1-month alongside eyelid treatment.

therapies_index.name: hyaluronic acid eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Used alone or with CsA in a retrospective comparison; a separate MGX study specified a 0.1% formulation.

therapies_index.name: 0.3% tobramycin/0.1 dexamethasone combined eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Given once a day as part of standard treatment in a study assessing the addition of MGX.

therapies_index.name: tobramycin
therapies_index.administration: Included in combined eye drops described as 0.3% tobramycin/0.1 dexamethasone; tobramycin and dexamethasone eye drops were also a comparator in a CsA study.

therapies_index.name: dexamethasone
therapies_index.administration: Included in combined eye drops described as 0.3% tobramycin/0.1 dexamethasone; tobramycin and dexamethasone eye drops were also a comparator in a CsA study.

therapies_index.name: antibiotics and corticosteroid-containing ophthalmic ointment
therapies_index.administration: Applied after probing in one study; the individual agents and schedule are not specified.

therapies_index.name: lubricant ointment
therapies_index.administration: One probing study used an ointment containing dextran or a similar substance after probing and also studied lubricant ointment without probing.

therapies_index.name: dextran
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned as a constituent of lubricant ointment used after probing.

therapies_index.name: lifitegrast®
therapies_index.administration: Integrin-antagonist eye drops served as a comparator for LipiFlow® in one study; the schedule is not given.

therapies_index.name: epinephrine eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Long-term administration of 2% eye drops was described in a rabbit model, not as MGD treatment.
key_toxicities: The cited animal experiments produced meibomian duct dilation and obstructive changes after long-term use.

therapies_index.name: isotretinoin
therapies_index.administration: Systemic administration was discussed as a cause of meibomian gland changes in rabbits, not as MGD treatment. The guideline states that it was not approved in Japan for refractory acne.
key_toxicities: The cited rabbit experiments associated systemic administration with meibomian duct dilation.

therapies_index.name: rosiglitazone
therapies_index.mechanism: Identified as a PPAR-γ agonist; addition to cultured mouse meibocytes increased production of wax esters and cholesterol esters.
therapies_index.administration: Discussed only in a cell-culture experiment, not as clinical MGD treatment.

therapies_index.name: glaucoma eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned as exposure associated with MGD development, not as MGD treatment.
key_toxicities: Long-term use was reported to be associated with MGD.

recommendations.statement: Use shared diagnostic criteria when studying MGD prevalence or comparing diagnostic assessments and treatment effects; internationally consistent criteria covering high-delivery MGD and other subtypes are needed.
recommendations.rationale: Studies use differing combinations of symptoms, eyelid findings, meibum characteristics, and meibography, which limits comparison of their results.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ1 What are the diagnostic criteria for MGD?

recommendations.statement: When MGD is suspected, ask patients about ocular discomfort, foreign body sensation, dryness, pressure, pain, burning, tearing, eyestrain, blurred vision, itching, discharge, and photophobia; do not rely on a particular symptom to distinguish MGD from other ocular surface disorders.
recommendations.rationale: There is no convincing evidence that a characteristic subjective symptom differentiates MGD from other ocular surface disorders.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ2 What are the characteristic subjective symptoms of MGD and appropriate ways to elicit them from patients?

recommendations.statement: Assess meibomian gland orifice changes, eyelid margin vascularity, MCJ displacement, and eyelid margin irregularity as anatomical findings useful for diagnosing and classifying the severity of MGD.
recommendations.context: CQ3; usefulness for diagnosing high-delivery MGD is not sufficiently established.
recommendations.rationale: These eyelid margin changes can be scored by their presence and extent.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ3 Is anatomical observation of the eyelid margins useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not use BUT as a test specifically diagnostic of MGD.
recommendations.rationale: Although BUT is often shorter in MGD than in normal eyes, it is unclear whether the change reflects gland abnormalities or associated dry eye.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ4 Is the measurement of BUT useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: BUP may serve as an auxiliary examination for MGD diagnosis, but the evidence is too limited and uncertain to determine whether its use should be recommended.
recommendations.rationale: BUP helps identify dry eye subtypes, but a pattern specific to MGD has not been reported.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ5 Is the observation of BUP helpful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Examine meibum with slit-lamp microscopy when diagnosing MGD, assessing its quality and expressibility semi-quantitatively.
recommendations.rationale: MGD changes both the amount and the characteristics of meibomian gland secretions.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ6 Is it useful to observe meibomian gland secretions in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not currently recommend NIBUT measurement as a diagnostic test for MGD.
recommendations.rationale: The few available studies disagree, and a standardized diagnostic cut-off has not been established.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ7 Is NIBUT measurement useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Use meibography to assist in diagnosing MGD.
recommendations.context: CQ8; gland morphology does not necessarily indicate ocular surface function.
recommendations.rationale: Meibography supports diagnosis while being noninvasive and quick, although device performance and image analyses differ.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ8 Is meibography useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Interpret LLT from tear interference imaging cautiously; its possible diagnostic usefulness for MGD requires a validated cut-off, and the diagnostic usefulness of interference patterns remains undetermined.
recommendations.rationale: LLT has been reported to be thinner in MGD, but tear reservoir volume and lipid-layer dynamics can affect the measurement.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ9 Is the observation of tear interference images useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not currently recommend measuring tear evaporation to diagnose MGD.
recommendations.rationale: Despite reports of increased evaporation in oMGD compared with healthy individuals, equipment and measurement conditions lack standardization and the test is not commonly used clinically.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ10 Is tear evaporation measurement useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Leave the decision to use IVCM in an individual clinical examination to the ophthalmologist; its use for MGD diagnosis cannot currently be recommended or ruled out.
recommendations.rationale: The identity of structures interpreted as meibomian acini requires confirmation, and contact with the epithelium and prolonged examination impose burdens on patients.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ11 Is IVCM useful in diagnosing MGD?

recommendations.statement: Tear film osmolality measurement need not be avoided, but its present clinical usefulness for diagnosing MGD is limited.
recommendations.rationale: Studies disagree about diagnostic effectiveness, although the test is minimally invasive.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ12 Is measuring tear film osmolality useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not regard eyelid margin lipid quantification as an established useful diagnostic test for MGD at present.
recommendations.rationale: The measurement has relatively little patient burden and can be reproduced semi-quantitatively, but no diagnostic cut-off has been established.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ13 Is lipid quantification on eyelid margins useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not use biochemical analysis of meibum as a current clinical diagnostic method for MGD.
recommendations.context: CQ14; further research may help clarify disease mechanisms and develop treatments.
recommendations.rationale: MGD-specific markers and analytical methods have not been established, while analysis and sample collection impose time, cost, and patient burdens.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ14 Is a biochemical analysis of the meibomian gland secretions useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not currently use tear inflammatory biomarker measurement to diagnose MGD, although it may eventually support adjunctive diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: The available findings have not established a biomarker sufficiently specific for MGD.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ15 Is measuring inflammatory biomarkers in tears useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Do not use bacteriological culture or polymerase chain reaction-based genomic testing as current diagnostic tests for MGD.
recommendations.rationale: Neither approach has produced findings characteristic of MGD.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ16 Are bacteriological tests useful in the diagnosis of MGD?

recommendations.statement: Use fluorescein as the most versatile stain for keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders in MGD; Rose Bengal and lissamine green are also used.
recommendations.context: CQ17; the distribution of affected epithelial sites in MGD has not been systematically characterized.
recommendations.source_heading: Q17 What are the frequency and characteristics of keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders in MGD and what are the appropriate staining methods?

recommendations.statement: Implement eyelid warming as a treatment for MGD.
recommendations.evidence_level: A (strong): Strongly confident in estimate of effect
recommendations.rationale: It improves subjective symptoms and meibum conditions, including meibum grade; the devices assessed were inexpensive and reusable.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ18 Is eyelid warming effective?

recommendations.statement: Implement eyelid hygiene for MGD, with caution about non-serious adverse effects that may depend on the cleansing agent.
recommendations.context: CQ19; water-moistened cotton may improve symptoms and BUT, while commercial cleansing agents may also improve gland findings, meibum grade, and epithelial damage.
recommendations.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effects
recommendations.rationale: Evidence for eyelid hygiene alone is limited, and the studies used differing cleansing methods.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ19 Is eyelid hygiene effective?

recommendations.statement: Offer MGX as a treatment option for oMGD.
recommendations.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimated effect
recommendations.rationale: MGX improves subjective symptoms, but MGX alone has not consistently improved objective findings, and compression-related pain burdens patients.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ20 Is meibomian gland expression effective?

recommendations.statement: Do not implement DQS eye drops as a treatment for MGD alone.
recommendations.context: CQ21; in patients who have both MGD and dry eye, DQS may improve symptoms and several clinical findings, but its efficacy in MGD without dry eye is unknown.
recommendations.evidence_level: C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effect
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed studies involved concurrent dry eye, and JHI does not cover DQS for MGD alone.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ21 Are diquafosol eye drops effective?

recommendations.statement: Implement azithromycin eye drops for MGD, while accounting for relatively frequent but mild adverse events.
recommendations.evidence_level: B (medium): Moderately confident in estimate of effect
recommendations.rationale: They improve symptoms, meibomian gland orifice and surrounding findings, and meibum grade; their effects on BUT and epithelial disorders are more limited.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ22 Are antimicrobial eye drops effective?

recommendations.statement: No clear recommendation can be made for ophthalmic ointments other than corticosteroid-based ointments or for lipid-containing eye drops in MGD.
recommendations.strength: Unable to make a clear recommendation.
recommendations.evidence_level: D (very weak): Little confidence in estimate of effect
recommendations.rationale: Only a limited number of the available formulations have been evaluated, with little evidence for each type.
recommendations.source_heading: CQ23 Are ophthalmic ointments (excluding corticosteroid-based ophthalmic ointment)/ oily eye drops effective?

recommendations.statement: Topical corticosteroid eye drops are marginally recommended for MGD, subject to the limits of the evidence and JHI coverage. The reviewed studies combined them with eyelid hygiene and warming, or combined corticosteroid and antibiotic eye drops with eyelid hygiene.

artifacts.title: Abstract of the Guidelines

rows: What is the pathophysiology of MGD?
Low-delivery MGD chiefly involves ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization and acinar atrophy; atrophy may arise primarily with aging or follow obstruction. High-delivery MGD remains poorly understood.
What are the definitions, classifications and severity staging of MGD?
MGD comprises low-delivery and high-delivery types. Reported subdivisions and severity classifications differ, without worldwide agreement.
What disorders are related to MGD?
Associated disorders include posterior blepharitis, meibomitis and ocular surface epithelial disease; their relationships matter in assessment and treatment.
What is the prevalence of MGD?

Diagnostic differences affect reported prevalence. A Japanese population study found 0% at 6–19 years, 11.8% at 20–29 years, 5.6% at 30–39 years, 21.6% at 40–49 years, 32.8% at 50–59 years, 41.9% at 60–69 years, 48.4% at 70–79 years and 63.9% at 80–96 years.
What factors are associated with development of MGD?
Reported factors include aging, male sex, postmenopausal status, Asian ethnicity, rural residence, VDT-related work, smoking, SCL use and glaucoma eye drops; ocular surgery has also been associated.
What systemic factors and disorders are associated with development of MGD?

Diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and hyperthyroidism are reported risks. Rosacea with ocular inflammation, SS, SJS and GVHD are likely associated; menopause and androgen deficiency are also related.
What are the diagnostic criteria for MGD?
Japanese criteria proposed in 2010 are often used for low-delivery MGD; globally accepted criteria have not been established.
What subjective symptoms characterize MGD and how should they be elicited?

Ask patients about ocular discomfort, foreign body sensation, dryness, pressure, pain, burning, tearing, fatigue, blurred vision, itching, discharge and photophobia. Symptoms alone have not been shown to distinguish MGD from other ocular surface disorders.
Is eyelid-margin anatomy useful for diagnosing MGD?
Useful findings are obstructed gland openings, margin vascularity, displaced MCJ and margin irregularity.
Is BUT useful for diagnosing MGD?
BUT is often shorter in MGD than in normal eyes, but does not specifically establish MGD.
Is BUP observation useful for diagnosing MGD?
BUP may support diagnosis, but an MGD-specific pattern has not been established.
Is observing gland secretions useful for diagnosing MGD?
Quantity and quality of meibum change in MGD; slit-lamp observation is recommended.
Is NIBUT useful for diagnosing MGD?
Limited studies and absence of an established cutoff prevent recommending NIBUT for this diagnostic purpose.
Is meibography useful for diagnosing MGD?
Meibography is recommended; it assesses gland morphology without invasion and takes little time.
Are tear interference images useful for diagnosing MGD?
LLT may be thinner in MGD, but diagnostic cutoffs require further investigation.
Is measuring tear evaporation useful for diagnosing MGD?
Increased evaporation has been reported in oMGD, but equipment and conditions lack standardization; measurement cannot currently be recommended.
Is IVCM useful for diagnosing MGD?
Published findings suggest utility, but identification of the imaged acini requires confirmation and invasiveness and examination burden require consideration.
Is tear film osmolality useful for diagnosing MGD?
Studies disagree about diagnostic utility. Its use is not ruled out, but present clinical usefulness is limited.
Is eyelid-margin lipid quantification useful for diagnosing MGD?
Despite relatively reproducible semi-quantitation and little patient burden, an absent cutoff limits diagnostic benefit.
Is biochemical analysis of meibum useful for diagnosing MGD?
MGD-specific analytical methods and markers have not been established; diagnostic benefit is lacking.
Are tear inflammatory biomarkers useful for diagnosing MGD?
They are not currently diagnostically useful, although adjunctive potential remains.
Are bacteriological tests useful for diagnosing MGD?
Cultures and genomic testing have not yielded characteristic diagnostic results.
What are the characteristics of epithelial disorders and suitable staining methods?
Systematic descriptions of lesion distribution are lacking. Fluorescein is the most useful stain; Rose Bengal and lissamine green are also used.
Water-moistened cotton may improve symptoms and BUT; commercial cleansers may improve additional gland and surface findings, although mild adverse effects can occur.
Potential benefit concerns MGD accompanied by dry eye; efficacy without dry eye is unknown, and JHI does not cover treatment of MGD alone.
Azithromycin improves symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, and meibum grade; adverse events are comparatively frequent but mild.
Are ophthalmic ointments other than corticosteroids or oily eye drops effective?
Evidence for individual preparations is too limited for a clear recommendation.
Not recommended due to insufficient evidence
Combined treatment with warming and hygiene may improve symptoms and findings, but evidence is limited and JHI does not cover MGD alone.
Benefits appear limited, and they are not considered an evidence-based MGD treatment.
Are oral omega-3 fatty acids effective?
May improve symptoms, vascularity near gland openings and BUT; MGD use is not covered by JHI.
Azithromycin, doxycycline and minocycline may improve symptoms and gland-opening findings; MGD treatment is not covered by JHI.
Improves several symptoms and examination outcomes with generally infrequent, mild, reversible adverse events; lack of Japanese approval and JHI coverage limits the final recommendation.
Improves symptoms and selected gland and tear-film findings, but lacks JHI coverage.
May improve symptoms in oMGD but seldom improves objective findings and is invasive.

rows: Develop evidence-based guidance, following MINDS as closely as possible, to assist decisions about MGD diagnosis and treatment.

The attending physician and patient make the final decision. Consider clinical circumstances, applicability to the patient, clinician expertise, facilities and insurance constraints; some treatments lack JHI coverage. Evidence includes publications through June 2021.

12 ophthalmologists, including the five supervisory members.

On October 8, 2020, the supervisory board agreed on the guideline framework. On December 27, 2020, the preparation team discussed pathophysiology, related disorders, SR methods and treatment evaluation.
January–June 2021: teams and responsibilities were selected, COI declarations collected, and scope, BQs and CQs finalized.
July 1, 2021: agreement with the Japan Medical Library Association. August 31, 2021: literature-search results received. September 2021 – March 2022: recommendations developed and discussed.
April 8, 12, and 19, 2022: recommendation text discussed. Treatment recommendation strengths were decided through a modified Delphi process and majority vote.
May–June 2022: external review informed revision and finalization.

document_sections.heading: Preface
document_sections.content: MGD is a functional disturbance of the meibomian glands that causes chronic ocular discomfort and can contribute to dry eye, including dryness and fatigue. Japanese surveys estimate MGD-related disorders in about 10–30% of people aged >50 years. The condition can reduce quality of life. The MGD Working Group published a definition, classification and diagnostic criteria in 2010, but that work was not comprehensive. The International Workshop on MGD published a broad assessment in 2011, although it relied on authority rather than an evidence-based guideline process. Following the MINDS method, this guideline addresses six BQs and 30 CQs through literature review and SR where appropriate. Its development identified many questions with limited reliable evidence; future research is expected to inform revision.

document_sections.heading: Explanation of Key Terms
document_sections.content: A meibocyte is a meibomian acinar cell, and meibum is the gland's secretion. Meibum grade is a semiquantitative assessment of secretion quality and expressibility used to assess MGD severity and treatment effects. In the Shimazaki approach, 0 denotes clear secretion expressed easily; 1, turbid secretion released with light compression; 2, turbid secretion requiring moderate compression; and 3, secretion that cannot be expressed even with strong compression. PPAR-γ is a transcription-acting nuclear receptor involved in adipocyte differentiation and lipid synthesis; it also contributes to meibocyte differentiation and lipid production. BUT measures the interval from eyelid opening until tear-film breakup; a shorter interval indicates less stable tears. It is commonly measured after fluorescein instillation, whereas NIBUT tracks changes over time in reflected projected light. Findings around gland orifices include vascularity, MCJ displacement and an irregular eyelid margin. Obstructive orifice findings result from accumulated keratinized material and include plugging, pouting and ridges. Obstructive meibomian gland dysfunction is a low-delivery subtype with diffuse orifice occlusion. Atrophic meibomian gland dysfunction is a low-delivery subtype with diffuse acinar atrophy, which may follow pressure from retained material or arise from effects on gland cells themselves.

document_sections.heading: Abstract of the Guidelines
document_sections.content: The summary covers six BQs on mechanisms, classification, associated disorders, prevalence and risk factors, followed by 30 CQs on diagnosis and treatment. Low-delivery MGD principally involves ductal hyperkeratinization and acinar atrophy; atrophy may be primary with aging or secondary to obstruction. High-delivery mechanisms remain poorly understood. Low- and high-delivery subtypes are recognized, but severity classifications lack worldwide agreement. MGD relates to posterior blepharitis, meibomitis and ocular-surface epithelial disease. A Japanese population study spanning ages 6–96 years reported age-group prevalence of 0% (6–19 years), 11.8% (20–29 years), 5.6% (30–39 years), 21.6% (40–49 years), 32.8% (50–59 years), 41.9% (60–69 years), 48.4% (70–79 years) and 63.9% (80–96 years). Reported risk factors include aging, male sex, postmenopausal status, Asian ethnicity, rural residence, VDT-related work, smoking, SCL use and glaucoma eye drops; ocular surgery has also been associated with MGD. Diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and hyperthyroidism are systemic risk factors. Rosacea with ocular inflammation, SS, SJS and GVHD are likely associated; menopause and androgen deficiency are also related. The Japanese low-delivery diagnostic criteria proposed in 2010 are commonly used, but no worldwide standard exists. Patients suspected of MGD should be asked about discomfort, foreign-body sensation, dryness, pressure, pain, burning, tearing, fatigue, blurred vision, itching, discharge and photophobia; symptoms alone have not been shown to distinguish MGD from other ocular-surface disorders. Useful eyelid findings include orifice obstruction, vascularity, MCJ displacement and margin irregularity. BUT is often shorter in MGD but does not specifically diagnose it. BUP may assist diagnosis, although no MGD-specific pattern is established. Slit-lamp evaluation of meibum and meibography are recommended. NIBUT cannot currently be recommended as an MGD diagnostic test. LLT measured through tear interference images might become useful after validation of a cutoff. Tear evaporation measurement is not recommended under current measurement conditions. IVCM use requires consideration of uncertainty about the imaged acinar structures, invasiveness and examination burden; the individual ophthalmologist should decide whether to use it. Tear osmolality currently has limited clinical utility. Eyelid-margin lipid quantification, biochemical meibum analysis, tear inflammatory biomarkers and bacteriological testing currently offer little or no diagnostic benefit. Fluorescein is the principal stain for keratoconjunctival epithelial abnormalities; Rose Bengal and lissamine green are also used. For treatment, eyelid warming is strongly recommended, while eyelid hygiene and MGX receive marginal recommendations for implementation. DQS is marginally recommended not to be implemented for MGD treatment because efficacy without dry eye is unknown and JHI does not cover MGD alone. Azithromycin eye drops, topical corticosteroids, oral n-3 fatty acids, oral azithromycin, oral doxycycline and oral minocycline receive marginal recommendations for implementation, subject to the qualifications in their respective CQs. Evidence is insufficient for a clear recommendation on non-corticosteroid ophthalmic ointments and lipid-containing eye drops. CsA eye drops and probing receive marginal recommendations not to be implemented. IPL has favorable efficacy and safety evidence, but its final recommendation is marginal implementation because it is not approved for MGD in Japan and lacks JHI coverage. Thermal pulsation likewise receives a marginal implementation recommendation because it lacks JHI coverage.

document_sections.heading: How to read and interpret the recommendations and explanations in this guideline
document_sections.content: This part explains the question format, evidence assessment and interpretation of recommendations.

document_sections.heading: The guidelines
document_sections.content: The guideline aims to give evidence-based recommendations in the Minds format when feasible. Important clinical issues are formulated as BQs and CQs and assessed through SR. Relevant issues unsuitable for SR receive a literature-based review. Topics bridging basic research and clinical care are treated separately as specific topics.

document_sections.heading: BQs and CQs
document_sections.content: Six BQs address pathophysiology, classification, related diseases, epidemiology and risk factors; 30 CQs address diagnosis, examination and treatment. BQs 1–3 are reviews. BQs 4–6 and CQs 1–17 are organized around recommendations, explanations, problems or bias, future issues and trends. Treatment CQs 18–30 additionally present recommendation strength, evidence strength, the basis for recommendations and SR summaries.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Answers to the BQs and CQs were developed from SR findings, outcome-specific evidence and the balance of benefits and harms. Patient preferences and economic considerations were also taken into account. Major treatment outcomes comprise symptoms, gland orifice and adjacent findings, secretion grade, BUT, epithelial disorders and adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Explanation, problem/bias, future issues, and trends
