document_sections.content: For BQs 4–6 and diagnostic CQs 1–17, the discussion addresses interpretation, bias and future research. CQs 1–17 assessed diagnostic usefulness, not usefulness for measuring MGD severity or response to treatment.

document_sections.heading: Strength of recommendation
document_sections.content: Recommendation strength was decided by votes of 12 committee members; members with COI for a CQ did not vote on that CQ. The implementation categories are Strongly recommend “implementation”, Marginally recommend “implementation”, Marginally recommend “not to be implemented” and Strongly recommend “not to be implemented”. When evidence could not support a conclusion, the designation was not recommended due to insufficient evidence.

document_sections.heading: Strength of evidence for CQ
document_sections.content: Outcome-level assessments were combined into an evidence-strength judgment for each CQ. The levels are A (strong), indicating strong confidence in the effect estimate; B (medium), moderate confidence; C (weak), limited confidence; and D (very weak), little confidence.

document_sections.heading: Process of developing recommendations
document_sections.content: Each CQ account describes how its recommendation was reached and which literature was considered. RCTs were the principal evidence source, with other relevant study types included when appropriate.

document_sections.heading: SR summary
document_sections.content: The SR assessed study-level evidence and bias and judged the overall evidence. Articles about posterior blepharitis or meibomitis were eligible when their clinical content was considered equivalent to MGD. Principal treatment outcomes were symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, secretion grade, BUT, epithelial disorders and adverse events. A recommendation was lowered when improvement appeared only in BUT and epithelial findings. Reported supplementary measures, including meibography, confocal microscopy, biochemical and bacterial tests, tear interference images and evaporation measurements, contributed to the overall assessment.

document_sections.heading: Preparation Process
document_sections.content: The guidelines were prepared to support diagnostic and treatment decisions for people involved in MGD care, following the MINDS method as closely as possible. They support, rather than replace, clinician judgment and shared decisions with patients. Application should take account of the clinical setting, individual symptoms and findings, clinician expertise, facility resources and insurance restrictions. Some recommended approaches lack JHI coverage and may require informed consent and, depending on the facility, ethical review. The evidence base covers medical articles published through June 2021; the guidance requires continued reassessment as evidence evolves. Members with relevant COI were excluded from voting on treatment CQs 18–30. The supervisory board consisted of five ophthalmologists; the preparation team had 12 ophthalmologists, including those five, and the SR team had 30 ophthalmologists, including the 12 preparation-team members. Development included preparation and scope-setting in 2020 and January–June 2021, literature searching and evidence synthesis in 2021–March 2022, modified Delphi discussion and majority voting on treatment recommendation strength in April 2022, and external evaluation and revision in May–June 2022.

document_sections.heading: Definitions, classifications, and diagnostic criteria
document_sections.content: The guideline retains the 2010 Japanese definition of MGD as diffuse meibomian gland dysfunction from various causes accompanied by chronic ocular discomfort. It revises classification and diagnostic criteria. Low-delivery MGD now comprises congenital, obstructive and atrophic categories; obstructive and atrophic disease may each be primary or secondary. Obstruction can arise through ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization, whereas atrophy can involve abnormal meibocytes, and obstructive disease may progress to atrophy. Distinguishing obstruction from atrophy can guide treatment strategy. Potential secondary causes listed with the classification are ageing, allergic eye disease, blepharitis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, pemphigus oculus, graft-versus-host disease, Sjögren's syndrome, trachoma, drug-induced disorders, chemical wounds and burns. High-delivery MGD remains a separate category because its mechanisms are insufficiently established; diagnostic criteria are therefore specified only for low-delivery disease. Those criteria require subjective symptoms together with abnormalities of the eyelid margins and of secretion quantity or quality. Either diffuse orifice obstruction or reduced expression or expression of viscous meibum on eyelid compression satisfies the latter criterion. If both obstruction and secretion abnormalities occur, oMGD is diagnosed; reduced lipid expression without the obstruction finding can indicate atrophic MGD. Symptoms clearly caused by a different ocular-surface disorder must not be counted toward MGD diagnosis. Vascularity or redness near orifices, MCJ displacement, margin irregularity, gland dropout on meibography, corneal changes, and abnormalities of BUT or BUP aid subtype identification, severity assessment and differential diagnosis but are not essential diagnostic criteria. The classification and diagnostic-criteria tables set out these revised categories and requirements.

document_sections.heading: Scope
document_sections.content: The chapter describes MGD clinical features, epidemiology, treatment and the intended reach and methods of the guideline.

document_sections.heading: I Clinical features
document_sections.content: The meibomian glands are sebaceous glands of the upper and lower tarsal plates. Their secretion reaches the tear surface through approximately 30–40 upper-lid and 20–30 lower-lid orifices. Meibum includes non-polar and polar lipids and is believed to support tear-film stability; the extent to which it prevents evaporation remains under investigation. MGD mechanisms are incompletely understood and differ between low- and high-delivery disease. Conventionally, ductal hyperkeratinization was thought to make meibum cloudy and viscous, obstruct its exit and reduce delivery. Aging, inflammation, hormonal imbalance, bacterial growth, eye drops and oral drugs may contribute; altered meibocytes have also been proposed as a core mechanism. High-delivery disease has been associated with inflammation and an increased amount of qualitatively abnormal expressed meibum, but its detailed mechanism remains unresolved.

document_sections.heading: 2. Clinical Classification
document_sections.content: The Japanese MGD Working Group's 2010 scheme separated low- from high-delivery disease and further distinguished primary and secondary forms; the 2011 TFOS MGD International Workshop instead separated low-delivery disease into hyposecretory and obstructive forms. High-delivery MGD may occur with rosacea or seborrheic dermatitis or be idiopathic. Its secretion can be increased yet qualitatively abnormal, so increased output does not imply normal gland function. This guideline revises the earlier Japanese classification.

document_sections.heading: 3. Definition and diagnostic criteria
document_sections.content: The Japanese 2010 definition centers on diffuse abnormal gland function and chronic ocular discomfort; the 2011 TFOS definition additionally refers to duct obstruction, altered secretion and potential tear-film and ocular-surface consequences. Prior studies applied different diagnostic criteria, ranging from eyelid-margin vascularity alone to combinations of vascularity, orifice obstruction and reduced secretion. The 2010 Japanese low-delivery criteria required symptoms, abnormalities surrounding the orifices and orifice obstruction. The preparation team considered revision necessary after 12 years of developments in disease understanding and treatment; the revised criteria appear earlier in the guideline.

document_sections.heading: II Epidemiological characteristics
document_sections.content: Japanese surveys estimate MGD prevalence at about 10–30% among people aged ≥50 years, although its exact prevalence remains uncertain. Reports suggest higher prevalence in Asian than Western populations, with low-delivery disease predominating in Japan and high-delivery disease relatively more frequent in Western countries. Orifice obstruction or reduced secretion without symptoms may represent a precursor state. Studies report 11–18% symptomatic MGD and 30–63% asymptomatic MGD, but distinguishing symptom-free MGD findings from aging is difficult; early treatment in the absence of symptoms is therefore controversial. Reported risk factors include aging, menopause, androgen depletion, dyslipidemia, prostatic hypertrophy, contact-lens use and Demodex.

document_sections.heading: III Treatment of MGD
document_sections.content: Assessment commonly begins with symptoms and history, followed by examinations including visual acuity and intraocular pressure. Slit-lamp findings at and around gland orifices and changes in meibum support diagnosis. BUT, BUP and keratoconjunctival epithelial findings help assess associated dry eye; meibography and tear-film interferometry can provide further support. Treatment rests on eyelid hygiene, warming and expression of retained meibum. Inflammatory findings prompt anti-inflammatory treatment with eye drops or oral medication. Concurrent dry eye is treated with drops according to its type and severity. The relevant diagnostic and therapeutic questions are addressed in CQs 2–17 and CQs 18–30, respectively.

document_sections.heading: IV Scope of the proposed clinical practice guidelines
document_sections.content: The guideline seeks to support evidence-based decisions about MGD treatment by ophthalmologists, other healthcare personnel and patients. It applies to all patients affected by MGD. Its clinical questions address mechanisms, classification, severity, associated conditions, epidemiology and risk; useful diagnostic tests; and treatment efficacy and safety. Treatment evaluation considers symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, tear-film stability, corneal and conjunctival epithelial disease, and adverse events. Topics suitable for evidence assessment were selected as BQs and CQs; relevant topics unsuitable for SR received a literature review.

document_sections.heading: V Systematic review
document_sections.content: SR preparation, searching, screening and integration took place between January–February 2021 and April 2021–March 2022. Searches were supported by the Japan Medical Library Association and used PubMed, Ichushi-Web and The Cochrane Library. The literature period was January 1995–June 2021. RCTs were preferred; relevant non-RCTs could be selected when qualifying RCTs were absent or scarce. Overall evidence strength was assessed using the MINDS Guide for Developing Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017.

document_sections.heading: VI Preparation, finalization, and public release of recommendations
document_sections.content: The preparation team used overall evidence reports to formulate answers to BQs and CQs. Evidence strength was classified as A (strong), B (medium), C (weak) or D (very weak). Recommendation strength additionally reflected benefit–harm balance, patient values and economic perspectives. External reviewers evaluated the draft, after which the teams considered and incorporated revisions before finalization.

document_sections.heading: BQ1 What is the pathophysiology of MGD?
document_sections.content: Meibum supplies the superficial tear-film lipid layer. The reported composition includes wax esters 30–48%, cholesterol esters 30–40%, (O-acyl) -ω-hydroxy fatty acid 1–5%, cholesterol 0.5% and free fatty acids 0.1–1%. Its contribution to tear stability is accepted, but the model that MGD causes dry eye primarily by increasing aqueous evaporation is disputed. MGD is better considered a group of meibomian-gland-related pathological states than a single disease. Clinical signs can include eyelid-margin vascularity, plugging and meibum that becomes yellow or white, turbid, granular, viscous or toothpaste-like. The 2011 MGD International Workshop described ductal hyperkeratinization and viscous meibum causing orifice obstruction and reduced drainage, with subsequent acinar atrophy and reduced secretion. The guideline also recognizes primary abnormalities of meibocytes as a possible core mechanism.

document_sections.heading: Low-delivery MGD
document_sections.content: Low-delivery disease encompasses impaired outflow, sometimes called oMGD, and reduced secretion. Its principal pathological processes are ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization and acinar atrophy.

document_sections.heading: 1. Hyperkeratinization
document_sections.content: Excess keratinization of the gland duct can increase keratinized material in meibum, raise viscosity and obstruct secretion. Reports beginning in 1980 described keratotic occlusion in people with contact-lens intolerance; subsequent histopathology linked duct and orifice keratinization to obstruction and dilation. Experimental exposure to 2% epinephrine eye drops in rabbits, polychlorinated biphenyls in monkeys and isotretinoin in rabbits also produced duct dilation. Keratinized material has been identified in turbid meibum. These findings support hyperkeratinization as a major, though not exclusive, MGD mechanism.

document_sections.heading: 2. Acinar atrophy
document_sections.content: Atrophic acini are small and irregular, and their loss suggests reduced secretion. Atrophy may follow pressure from retained meibum, but aging may also cause primary meibocyte atrophy without ductal hyperkeratinization. A 2017 review proposed that PPAR-γ and meibocyte stem or progenitor cells may be affected by aging, inflammation, hormones, environmental stress, neural inputs and diet. PPAR-γ contributes to meibocyte differentiation and lipid synthesis; in cultured mouse meibocytes, rosiglitazone increased wax ester and cholesterol ester production. Stem and progenitor cells are thought to reside near the acinus–duct junction, although their location is disputed. Dysfunction of cells serving individual acini could account for gland dropout.

document_sections.heading: High-delivery MGD
document_sections.content: High-delivery MGD describes expression of a large volume of meibum and often accompanies seborrheic dermatitis, rosacea or acne vulgaris. Whether production genuinely increases or mildly obstructed secretion is released remains uncertain. Symptoms and eyelid-margin findings may be informative even when meibography reveals few structural changes. A proposed mechanism is that abundant lipid supports bacterial growth, after which bacterial lipases alter lipids and free fatty acids promote inflammation; this remains an explanation rather than an established account of all high-delivery disease.

document_sections.heading: Meibum abnormality
document_sections.content: Meibum contains more than 100 known lipids and has a melting range of 28–32°C. Studies report altered lipid amounts, composition and structure in MGD, potentially affecting lipid-layer flow and tear stability. One study found more unsaturated free fatty acids in cloudy or yellow than clear meibum; oxidation may contribute to color. Reports in MGD and older subjects describe fewer non-polar and more polar lipids, while triglycerides increased significantly only in MGD patients in one comparison. Meibum also contains proteins, including keratin. A Raman microscopy study found that the meibum lipid-to-protein ratio correlated with BUT. Lipid-composition findings can depend on analytical method, so further research is needed.

document_sections.heading: 1. Aging
document_sections.content: Multiple studies associate MGD with aging. Human and mouse findings suggest age-related acinar atrophy without necessarily involving ductal hyperkeratinization. Ki-67 positivity decreases with age, and the reported cellular distribution of PPAR-γ changes from cytoplasmic and nuclear staining in younger specimens to nuclear staining in older specimens. Reduced PPAR-γ activity has been proposed as a contributor to age-related atrophy.

document_sections.heading: 2. Sex hormones
document_sections.content: Androgens influence meibomian-gland biosynthesis, secretion, differentiation and proliferation. Reported gene-expression effects favor lipid metabolism and oppose epithelial keratinization. Experiments in immortalized human gland epithelial cells found that dihydrotestosterone reduced expression of several inflammatory cytokines.

document_sections.heading: 3. Inflammation
document_sections.content: Allergic conjunctivitis, rosacea, SJS and chemical burns can affect gland structure or function. Reports describe gland distortion in allergic conjunctivitis, dropout in phlyctenular keratitis and inflammatory infiltrates near glands. An allergic-eye-disease mouse model showed duct dilation and acinar atrophy, with a possible role for neutrophil extracellular traps. Bacterially associated meibomitis may accompany keratoconjunctivitis, with organisms and clinical manifestations varying by age. Further research is needed to define meibomitis through clinical assessment of gland inflammation.

document_sections.heading: 4. Microorganisms such as bacteria
document_sections.content: Bacteria may grow within glands or influence them from the conjunctival sac. Lipase-producing organisms identified in ocular samples include Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus, Corynebacterium and Cutibacterium acnes. A proposed pathway links bacterial lipid breakdown to altered tear lipids and free-fatty-acid-mediated inflammation. Reports associate Cutibacterium acnes with delayed hypersensitivity in the phlyctenular form of MRKC seen in younger people, and lipase-producing Staphylococcus with SPK in a non-phlyctenular form common in older people. Individual studies found more positive cultures or different conjunctival microbiota in MGD than controls, but the bacterial contribution remains uncertain. Meibum itself may have antimicrobial activity. Demodex folliculorum can parasitize eyelashes and cause marginal blepharitis; its relationship with MGD has been suggested but is not established.

document_sections.heading: 5. Environmental stress
document_sections.content: Meibography studies of contact-lens wearers found shorter glands and gland dropout. Desiccating-stress experiments in mice reported changes in Ki-67-positive cells, duct size and meibum protein-to-lipid ratio. In Cu, Zn-superoxide dismutase-1 knockout mice, studies found fibrosis, inflammation, lipid-droplet accumulation and age-related apoptosis around glands. These experimental observations suggest possible environmental and oxidative influences.

document_sections.heading: 6. Neural Factors
document_sections.content: Sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation and neuropeptides influence meibomian glands. Neural regulation of meibum secretion is proposed, but many details remain uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 7. Drugs
document_sections.content: Long-term epinephrine eye drops, systemic polychlorinated biphenyls and isotretinoin have been linked to MGD in the cited research. Long-term antiglaucoma eye drops have also been reported as a cause.

document_sections.heading: 8. Blinking
document_sections.content: Blinking distributes meibum across the ocular surface. Contraction and relaxation of the muscle of Riolan may assist secretion near gland orifices. Incomplete blinking has been reported as a contributor to MGD.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: The guideline proposes two principal mechanisms for low-delivery MGD: ductal epithelial hyperkeratinization and meibocyte abnormalities. Aging, androgens, infection, inflammation or allergy, and other factors may act on both ductal and acinar cells. MGD mechanisms remain complex and partly unresolved, warranting more precise evaluation and classification.

document_sections.heading: Tear film lipid layer function and evaporative dry eye: Discrepancy between basic findings and clinical experience
document_sections.content: The tear-film lipid layer contributes to tear stability, but whether its main function in humans is evaporation suppression or resistance to localized thinning has not been resolved. The TFOS classification identifies MGD as a principal cause of evaporative dry eye. Evidence for marked evaporation suppression came largely from rabbits, whose BUT can reach 30 minutes, compared with 15 seconds in humans. Rabbit studies reported lipid-layer evaporation inhibition of 93% and 75%, whereas an in vitro human tear-film model reported 6–8%. Human in vivo studies have nevertheless measured increased evaporation with MGD. During blinking, upward lipid movement helps form the tear film. Human meibum is normally more elastic than viscous, while MGD meibum becomes more viscosity-dominant; elasticity may help the layer resist breakup during localized aqueous thinning. An experiment in which temperature rose at constant humidity found greater evaporation alongside a thicker, more stable lipid layer, suggesting evaporation alone does not determine stability. If elasticity rather than evaporation suppression proves primary, the existing evaporative-dry-eye classification will need reconsideration.

document_sections.heading: BQ2 What are the definitions, classifications and severity staging of MGD?
document_sections.content: Published definitions and classifications are summarized in the chapter's tables. The Japanese MGD Working Group and TFOS MGD International Workshop provide explicit definitions. Both broadly distinguish low- and high-delivery disease, but proposed subdivisions differ. Severity schemes use symptoms, orifice obstruction, surrounding abnormalities, morphology, meibum expression and lipid characteristics, and meibography. No worldwide standardized severity classification exists.

document_sections.heading: Definition
document_sections.content: The Japanese 2010 definition emphasizes diffuse abnormal gland function from various causes accompanied by chronic discomfort. The 2011 TFOS definition emphasizes chronic diffuse gland abnormality, often involving terminal-duct obstruction or altered secretion, with possible tear-film, inflammatory and ocular-surface effects.

document_sections.heading: Classification
document_sections.content: Foulks et al. proposed a detailed low- and high-delivery classification in 2003, including hyposecretory and obstructive forms and several primary or disease-associated subtypes. The Japanese 2010 scheme also divided each broad type into primary and secondary forms. TFOS in 2011 distinguished hyposecretory and obstructive low-delivery forms. Randon et al. later proposed IVCM categories: type 0 for normal findings, type 1 for obstruction, type 2 for inflammation and type 3 for fibrosis. High-delivery disease can show symptoms and margin abnormalities resembling low-delivery disease but greater lipid expression with eyelid compression. A cited account additionally described normal tear dynamics, absence of gland dropout and meibum quantity ≥0.8 mm. These reported classifications are not interchangeable with the guideline's revised scheme.

document_sections.heading: Severity staging
document_sections.content: The 2011 TFOS MGD International Workshop proposed four severity stages using secretion characteristics, symptoms and corneal staining, with treatment suggestions by stage. The scheme has not become a worldwide standard. Guliani et al. proposed stages 1–4 from symptoms, slit-lamp findings and tear tests; Fu et al. proposed three stages using symptoms, IVCM, slit-lamp findings, meibography, BUT and staining. Tables summarize the published stages and clinical findings associated with severity.

document_sections.heading: Problems
document_sections.content: Definitions and classifications are broadly similar but lack global consistency. Severity staging is likewise not internationally uniform.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Internationally standardized MGD classification, severity staging and treatment remain to be established. Collaborative research is needed.

document_sections.heading: BQ3 What disorders are related to MGD?
document_sections.content: The gland's position at the eyelid margin helps explain links with marginal blepharitis and ocular-surface disorders. Distinguishing functional gland disease from eyelid inflammation and understanding meibomitis-related ocular-surface inflammation are important for diagnosis and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 1. Blepharitis, marginal blepharitis (anterior and posterior blepharitis)
document_sections.content: Blepharitis denotes eyelid inflammation; marginal blepharitis affects its margin. Anterior blepharitis affects tissue around the eyelash roots, often with collarettes. Posterior blepharitis affects tissue behind the gray line and can accompany MGD, conjunctivitis or rosacea. MGD may cause posterior blepharitis, but posterior blepharitis describes inflammation and is not synonymous with MGD. MGD is generally not classified as anterior blepharitis, although anterior inflammation can extend posteriorly.

document_sections.heading: 2. Meibomitis
document_sections.content: Meibomitis denotes inflammatory disorders involving the meibomian glands and does not cover all MGD, because MGD may occur without apparent inflammation. Japanese usage has particularly linked meibomitis to bacterial growth. Historical descriptions emphasized inflamed hypersecretory disease; later definitions also encompassed noninflamed oMGD. The term MRKC was proposed for meibomitis accompanied by ocular-surface inflammation.

document_sections.heading: 3. Meibomitis and ocular surface epithelial disorders
document_sections.content: The discussion covers meibomian keratoconjunctivitis, MRKC, ocular rosacea and related childhood inflammatory disorders, and chalazion. The relationships distinguish diffuse MGD from focal gland abnormalities while recognizing overlapping inflammation.

document_sections.heading: 1. Meibomian keratoconjunctivitis
document_sections.content: The condition proposed by McCulley and Sciallis in 1977 combines chronic blepharitis, retained gland secretion and SPK, which was thought to relate to tear-film instability. Anterior and posterior blepharitis and meibomitis were present; about 30% of patients also had rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.

document_sections.heading: 2. MRKC
document_sections.content: MRKC was first proposed in 2000 under an earlier name and renamed in 2007. It combines meibum stagnation and inflamed, swollen eyelid margins with corneal or conjunctival disease. Its phlyctenular form includes corneal infiltration and superficial vascularization; its non-phlyctenular form predominantly involves SPK without infiltration. Because meibomitis severity correlates with ocular-surface disease severity, antimicrobial treatment of meibomitis is considered essential. The phlyctenular form occurs predominantly in young women and has been attributed in reports to Cutibacterium acnes. The non-phlyctenular form occurs in young and older patients, with possible involvement of Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus species. In older people, its SPK can resemble dry-eye-related SPK. MRKC often accompanies oMGD.

document_sections.heading: 3. Ocular rosacea, blepharokeratoconjunctivitis, and phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis.
document_sections.content: Rosacea is characterized by facial erythema and vascularity and may accompany blepharitis, meibomitis and keratoconjunctivitis. It is less common in children and in Asian populations, including Japanese people. Severe corneal inflammation in children or young adults can be described as childhood ocular rosacea, pediatric blepharokeratoconjunctivitis or phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis, even without facial rosacea. The guideline places these meibomitis-associated ocular inflammatory presentations in the same disease category as MRKC and notes reported responses to systemic antimicrobials.

document_sections.heading: 4. Chalazion
document_sections.content: Chalazion is a focal chronic inflammatory lesion associated with retained meibum, usually with an obstructed orifice and absent secretion. Because MGD definitions require diffuse gland abnormality, chalazion is classified separately. It can nevertheless signal focal obstructive inflammation and be relevant when assessing MRKC or ocular rosacea.

document_sections.heading: Further issues
document_sections.content: Although prevailing MGD definitions require diffuse gland changes, focal obstruction and inflammation can produce ocular-surface disease, including phlyctenular MRKC. The possibility of focal MGD is raised but not established.

document_sections.heading: BQ4 What is the prevalence of MGD?
document_sections.content: Reported prevalence depends strongly on diagnostic criteria. A Japanese population-based study covering ages 6–96 years reported 0% (6–19 years), 11.8% (20–29 years), 5.6% (30–39 years), 21.6% (40–49 years), 32.8% (50–59 years), 41.9% (60–69 years), 48.4% (70–79 years) and 63.9% (80–96 years). Across cited studies, reported prevalence ranged from 3.5% to 74.5%. A comparison using the same diagnostic criteria among participants aged ≥50 years found, in Spain, 10.9% symptomatic, 21.4% asymptomatic and 32.3% combined MGD; the corresponding Japanese study reported 11.2%, 63.6% and 74.5%. These are findings of the cited studies, not directly comparable estimates from studies using different criteria. The prevalence table presents study populations, diagnostic measures and reported rates.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Differences in symptom requirements and clinical criteria substantially alter prevalence estimates; stricter criteria tend to yield lower estimates. Some examination findings are not wholly quantitative, so examiner judgments can differ. Symptom questionnaires and their thresholds vary. Few prevalence studies adequately excluded symptoms attributable to other ocular-surface disorders.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: International standardization is needed for diagnostic criteria, their component measures and symptom questionnaires. These tools should continue to be updated as disease mechanisms become clearer.

document_sections.heading: BQ5 What are the factors associated with the development of MGD?
document_sections.content: Numerous studies suggest that MGD becomes more frequent or severe with aging. Reported associations include male sex, postmenopausal status, Asian ethnicity, rural residence, VDT-related work, smoking, SCL use and glaucoma eye drops; ocular surgery has also been implicated. The cited Hirado–Takushima study found the highest prevalence at age ≥80 years. Sex findings are inconsistent across studies: some favor men or postmenopausal women, while others find no significant sex difference. Smoking findings likewise conflict. In a VDT-worker study, MGD was observed in 74.3% of the sample, and discomfort correlated significantly with working time among affected workers. Reports describe worsening after cataract and other ocular surgeries. Studies also associate MGD findings with ocular demodicosis, radiotherapy, an ocular prosthesis and eyeliner use. The risk-factor table collates the contributing studies, their diagnostic criteria and reported factors.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Study-to-study differences in MGD definitions and criteria, participant age and sex distributions may have influenced apparent risk-factor associations.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Evidence about racial and regional differences remains limited. Studies applying common MGD diagnostic criteria could help clarify those differences.

document_sections.heading: BQ6 What are the systemic factors and disorders associated with the development of MGD?
document_sections.content:
The recommendations section begins by identifying diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and hyperthyroidism as systemic conditions associated with MGD development. The accompanying systemic-risk-factor table lists studies, populations, assessed factors and findings.

The guideline identifies diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hyperthyroidism as systemic conditions associated with MGD. It considers rosacea with ocular inflammation, SS, SJS, and GVHD likely to be associated with its development. Menopause and androgen deficiency are also related. The accompanying table surveys studies of systemic risk factors.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Studies report diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia as MGD risk factors; the evidence implicating hyperlipidemia is particularly extensive. Altered systemic lipid metabolism may affect meibomian gland lipids, but that mechanism remains possible rather than established. Thyroid disorders are also associated with MGD, particularly hyperthyroidism and thyroid eye disease; ocular protrusion may physically affect the glands. Studies report strong associations with SS, GVHD, rosacea, and SJS, potentially involving glandular inflammation. Menopause, reduced androgen levels, and prostatic hypertrophy have likewise been reported as risk factors. Table 9 presents the underlying studies and their findings.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Variation in MGD definitions and diagnostic criteria across studies can bias diagnosis. Its overlap with dry eye leaves uncertain whether systemic conditions act directly on MGD or indirectly through dry eye. Most studies assess one systemic disease rather than several, so substantial uncertainty remains about systemic contributors.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trend
document_sections.content: Prospective investigations using standardized MGD definitions, pathophysiological concepts, and diagnostic criteria are needed to examine systemic risk factors through different approaches.

document_sections.heading: CQ1 What are the diagnostic criteria for MGD?
document_sections.content: Japan commonly uses criteria proposed for low-delivery MGD by the MGD working group in 2010, but no diagnostic criteria are internationally uniform. Studies use differing combinations of symptoms, eyelid-margin abnormalities, changes in meibum quantity and quality, and meibography findings. Common criteria would facilitate prevalence research and comparisons of treatments and assessment methods; internationally consistent criteria must also address other subtypes, including high-delivery MGD.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Of 33 diagnostic articles considered at secondary screening, 10 were selected; Table 10 identifies them. Japan’s 2010 criteria require symptoms, abnormalities around gland orifices, and orifice obstruction for low-delivery MGD; Table 11 sets out those historical criteria. The TFOS report gives characteristic findings and assessment methods rather than definitive diagnostic criteria. Its proposed outpatient evaluation covers symptoms, blinking, tear meniscus, osmolality if feasible, fluorescein BUT, ocular-surface staining, Schirmer test or phenol red thread test, and finally eyelid morphology, expressed meibum, and gland dropout. It also proposes stage-based management, summarized in Table 12. Differences between grading methods and independently devised study criteria obstruct comparisons. Seven selected clinical studies examined alternative diagnostic approaches, summarized in Table 13. Shimazaki et al. found low-delivery MGD in 64.6% of people with ocular discomfort; concurrent orifice obstruction and meibographic dropout accompanied significantly greater epithelial damage and tear evaporation. Arita et al. reported 68% sensitivity and 80% specificity for distinguishing low-delivery MGD from ADDE when symptoms, abnormal margins, and meiboscore were all required. Mathers et al. suggested that gland dropout, expressed-meibum quality and quantity, Schirmer results, and tear evaporation helped distinguish ocular disorders. Another Arita et al. study reported 84.9% sensitivity and 96.7% specificity when two of symptoms, eyelid-margin score, and meiboscore were abnormal. Giannaccare et al. reported 86.2% sensitivity and 38.5% specificity when either BUT ≤ 9.6 seconds or gland loss > 20% was present; requiring both gave 39.3% sensitivity and 85.6% specificity. Xiao et al. reported 93% sensitivity and 97% specificity using gland-dropout area, and 93% sensitivity and 90% specificity using distortion of six or more glands. For high-delivery MGD, Arita et al. reported 100% sensitivity and 96.7% specificity with subjective symptoms ≥ 2 and abnormal eyelid margins ≥ 2. Evidence remains insufficient to define clear standards for other MGD subtypes. The promising alternative criteria require further study.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Although studies follow broadly similar diagnostic concepts, their criteria, meibum-expression assessments, and scoring systems differ, hindering comparison. Criteria for subtypes other than low-delivery MGD remain unclear.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Internationally harmonized diagnostic criteria and assessment methods are desirable because their absence restricts comparisons of prevalence, diagnostic assessments, and treatment efficacy.

document_sections.heading: CQ2 What are the characteristic subjective symptoms of MGD and appropriate ways to elicit them from patients?
document_sections.content: When MGD is suspected, clinicians should ask about ocular discomfort, foreign body sensation, dryness, pressure, pain, burning, tearing, eyestrain, blurred vision, itching, discharge, and photophobia. Convincing evidence for symptoms that distinguish MGD from other ocular-surface disorders is currently lacking.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: The Japanese 2010 low-delivery MGD criteria include discomfort, foreign body sensation, dryness, and pressure. International workshop criteria also contemplate symptoms, while treating absence of symptoms as a possible preclinical stage. In a Japanese survey of people aged ≥50 undergoing cataract surgery, symptomatic MGD prevalence was 18.0% and asymptomatic MGD prevalence was 29.5%; dry-eye symptoms were stronger in symptomatic cases. Eyelid-related symptoms alone do not reliably differentiate MGD. Questionnaires used include McMonnies Questionnaire, Schein Questionnaire, OSDI, Dry Eye Questionnaire, Ocular Comfort Index, SPEED, and Dry Eye Related Quality of Life Score. Treatment studies have detected significant changes in questionnaire scores, but reported relationships between symptoms and clinical tests vary. Arita et al. reported the highest diagnostic area under the curve for an ocular-symptom score: 0.948 (95% confidence interval: 0.912–0.984). Fu et al. did not identify distinctive symptoms, although they suggested a relationship with inflammation. Paugh et al. reduced an assessment of frequency and severity across 12 symptoms and 24 items to seven symptoms and 14 items. Their resulting questionnaire correlated with the original Schein questionnaire, detected treatment effects, and did not correlate with BUT; they considered it specifically designed for MGD diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: No individual symptom has been established as diagnostic of MGD, and evidence about highly sensitive and specific symptoms is sparse. Studies support asking about symptoms and suggest possible symptom combinations, but their present diagnostic value remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Researchers should test the reproducibility and diagnostic and treatment-assessment value of potentially distinctive symptoms and symptom combinations.

document_sections.heading: CQ3 Is anatomical observation of the eyelid margins useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Useful findings include gland-orifice changes—plugging, pouting, capping, and ridges—together with eyelid-margin vascularity, MCJ displacement, and margin irregularity. Scoring their presence and extent helps diagnose and classify MGD severity. Evidence for this approach in high-delivery MGD is insufficient.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Five principal findings considered are margin vascularity, MCJ displacement, irregularity, thickness, and orifice changes. Diagnostic studies combine these findings differently. Seven articles examined irregularity, vascularity, plugging, and MCJ displacement; one examined irregularity, vascularity, thickness, and plugging; two examined irregularity, vascularity, and plugging; and two examined vascularity and plugging. Amano et al., studying 510 people, found differences between MGD and non-MGD groups for all four assessed margin findings under Spanish criteria (p <0.0001 for all four factors) and under the 2010 Japanese low-delivery criteria (p < 0.0001). A Chinese multicenter study of 2,900 participants found that a composite margin score correlated with its oMGD grade (p <0.001). In an Indian study of 570 people, each of four margin scores differed between MGD and non-MGD groups (p <0.001, respectively); after separating MGD cases by symptoms, only plugging differed significantly. Arita et al. compared 30 patients with oMGD and 20 healthy controls and used vascularity, irregularity, thickness, and plugging for grading, omitting MCJ anterior displacement despite a between-group difference. Whether MCJ displacement in MGD is anterior or posterior remains disputed. Anterior displacement has also been associated with conjunctivochalasis and other ocular-surface disorders. Evidence chiefly concerns low-delivery MGD. One high-delivery MGD study proposed a combined score of irregularity, vascularity, outer-canthus foaming, and MCJ displacement; diagnostic criteria for that subtype remain unsettled.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Countries use slightly different MGD criteria. Plugging and other obstructive findings are readily recognizable gland-related changes, whereas vascularity, irregularity, thickness, and MCJ displacement also occur in other eyelid or ocular-surface diseases. Their specificity for MGD has not been adequately established.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Further multicenter and intervention studies should apply consistent MGD criteria and compare eyelid anatomy with healthy controls and other ocular-surface diseases. High-delivery MGD requires separate investigation.

document_sections.heading: CQ4 Is the measurement of BUT useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Many studies find shorter BUT in MGD than in normal eyes. Whether this reflects meibomian abnormalities themselves or associated dry eye remains disputed, and findings concerning glandular morphology are inconsistent. BUT therefore does not specifically diagnose MGD.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Fluorescein BUT and non-fluorescein NIBUT assess tear-film stability; this question concerns fluorescein BUT. Table 14 organizes comparisons with normal eyes, non-MGD eyes, dry-eye subtypes, and gland-related findings. Some studies report significantly shorter BUT in MGD than in normal eyes or non-MGD groups, whereas others find no significant difference. Patient-selection differences may contribute. In patients with MGD, concurrent dry eye has been associated with significantly shorter BUT than MGD without dry eye. Comparisons with ADDE and other dry-eye subtypes conflict, as do studies relating BUT to gland morphology, MGD grade, gland loss, or tortuosity. Arita et al. ranked single-test discrimination of oMGD from normal eyes as symptoms, abnormal margins, meiboscore, then BUT; multiple parameters are consequently needed.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Inconsistent MGD definitions, examined eyelid regions, and assessment methods complicate comparisons. The Japanese dry-eye BUT cutoff is ≤5 seconds, whereas some studies use 7 or 10 seconds.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Tear volume, mucin, lipid layer, and corneal epithelial disorders can affect BUT and warrant evaluation alongside MGD. Environmental influences, including VDT work, also require further investigation.

document_sections.heading: CQ5 Is the observation of BUP helpful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: BUP can assist classification of dry-eye subtypes and may support MGD diagnosis, but no MGD-specific pattern has been reported. Because direct evidence is sparse and uncertain, the guideline cannot determine whether to recommend BUP for MGD diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: The Asia Dry Eye Society describes aqueous-deficient, decreased-wettability, and increased-evaporation dry-eye types. Fluorescein BUP offers clues to tear-film disturbance: area and line breaks indicate aqueous deficiency, spot and dimple breaks decreased wettability, and random breaks an evaporative pattern. Low-delivery MGD may impair the tear lipid layer, but random breaks are not specific because healthy eyes and other tear-film disorders can show them. Shigeyasu et al. assessed 867 eyes and found MGD in 16.9% of 117 eyes with random breaks. BUP in high-delivery MGD is unknown.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: BUP research chiefly addresses dry eye rather than MGD specifically. Because MGD can coexist with different dry-eye types, its BUP need not be a random break.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: BUP may characterize associated dry eye and provide auxiliary evidence of lipid-layer disturbance, but its diagnostic usefulness in MGD remains unestablished and needs further study.

document_sections.heading: CQ6 Is it useful to observe meibomian gland secretions in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: MGD changes meibum quantity and quality. The guideline recommends examining meibum with slit-lamp microscopy, principally through semiquantitative assessment of its appearance and expressibility.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Color, properties, and quantity should be observed in both delivery types, although evidence has not established a clear high-delivery assessment method. For low-delivery MGD, eyelid compression permits semiquantitative evaluation; reduced expression forms part of Japanese diagnostic criteria. Table 15 compares established methods. Bron et al. assign quality grades 0–3 to material from eight glands; scores may use the highest grade or a sum ranging 0–24. A summed score is generally recommended, but can fall when advanced obstruction stops secretion altogether. Pflugfelder et al. grade how many of five glands express secretion: 0 for all, 1 for 3-4, 2 for 1-2, and 3 for none. Korb and Blackie count glands producing liquid secretion under standardized pressure across nasal, central, and temporal sites; even healthy temporal glands express less than nasal glands. Shimazaki et al. combine secretion appearance with the compression needed, using grades 0–3. Of 23 articles considered at secondary screening, 17 included meibum observation: 10 used both Bron et al. and Pflugfelder et al. methods, one used Bron et al. alone, and six used Shimazaki et al. No internationally standardized approach exists; studies also differ in the eyelids and regions assessed.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Neither the assessment method nor eyelid sampling area is standardized. Reported differences between upper and lower eyelids and between nasal and temporal sites mean compression location can change results.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Comparable treatment and test studies require common methods of meibum expression, anatomical sampling, and grading.

document_sections.heading: CQ7 Is NIBUT measurement useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Few studies have examined NIBUT for MGD and their findings conflict, so its diagnostic usefulness cannot be determined. Despite being noninvasive, the test is available at few facilities and lacks a standardized MGD cutoff. It cannot currently be recommended for diagnosing MGD.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Fluorescein BUT is accessible and inexpensive, but fluorescein exposure, examiner technique, dye quantity, reproducibility, temperature, humidity, and air conditioning may affect results. NIBUT devices instead follow distortion of reflected projected light. Available examples include Keratograph5M ®, ICP Tearscope TM, idraTM, and DR-1αTM. Evidence for dry-eye diagnosis is greater than for MGD. Giannaccare et al. found significantly shorter NIBUT in MGD than in controls and reported a 9.6 seconds cutoff with 65.8% sensitivity and 63.0% specificity; NIBUT alone was inadequate. Kim et al., using another device, found no significant difference. Studies including dry eye likewise conflict: Qi et al. found shorter NIBUT in an MGD group, whereas Abdelfattah et al. found no group difference. Ji et al. reported shortening with greater MGD severity; Robin et al. found no difference between MGD and comparator ocular diseases. Differences in equipment and study populations remain unresolved.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: All identified studies were observational. One had substantial selection bias; MGD criteria and measurement equipment differed, and results were seriously inconsistent. Shorter NIBUT could reflect MGD directly or its associated dry eye. Dedicated equipment and the absence of a specified MGD cutoff further restrict clinical benefit.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Combining NIBUT with gland-function measures may improve diagnostic accuracy. Additional studies might support noninvasive equipment that assesses several parameters together.

document_sections.heading: CQ8 Is meibography useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: The guideline recommends meibography for MGD diagnosis because it depicts gland morphology noninvasively and quickly. Device-dependent performance and disagreement between image analyses require caution; morphological appearance need not represent ocular-surface function.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Meibography examines gland morphology, including structural dropout, tortuosity, shortening, altered gland course, orifice dimensions, and gland number. Infrared non-contact methods have enabled broader clinical use. Studies address group comparisons, associations with ocular-surface and tear findings, and diagnostic accuracy; Table 16 surveys them.

document_sections.heading: 1. Comparison of two groups, such as normal eye and dry eye
document_sections.content: Compared with normal eyes, studies report greater gland dropout and altered gland length, shape, or orifices in MGD. Structural loss has also been reported as more frequent in MGD than in other dry-eye or symptomatic non-MGD groups. Some studies associate symptomatic disease with more dropout or tortuosity than asymptomatic disease.

document_sections.heading: 2. Relationship between meibomian gland morphology and ocular surface findings and tear function
document_sections.content: Some studies relate gland dropout to BUT, symptoms, staining, Schirmer results, evaporation, and expressed meibum, while others report no association for several of these outcomes. Lin et al. relate tortuosity to eyelid abnormalities, meiboscores, and expressibility. Liang et al. report associations of gland length with symptoms and width with BUT. Daniel et al. found corneal staining associated with composite gland scores for both eyelids, but BUT and Schirmer associations only for the upper eyelid. Dogan et al. favor upper-eyelid examination for more consistent image assessment.

document_sections.heading: 3. Diagnostic ability of meibography in MGD
document_sections.content: Adil et al. reported 96.7% sensitivity and 85% specificity for meibographic findings. Arita et al. found diagnostic discrimination strongest for symptoms, followed by margin abnormalities and then meiboscore.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Studies differ in MGD recruitment criteria and imaging devices, whose results do not always agree. Semiquantitative assessment raises reproducibility concerns. What tissue changes meibographic dropout represents remains uncertain; if dropout is irreversible, its usefulness for monitoring treatment response may be limited.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Research should identify which imaging parameters aid diagnosis, severity assessment, and treatment selection, and establish device-specific diagnostic cutoffs.

document_sections.heading: CQ9 Is the observation of tear interference images useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Imaging studies report thinner LLT in MGD. It might assist diagnosis if further work establishes a cutoff, but tear reservoir volume, lipid-layer dynamics, and delayed clearance complicate interpretation. The diagnostic usefulness of interference patterns cannot yet be concluded.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Tear interference imaging noninvasively assesses the surface lipid layer; some instruments also measure LLT. Devices available in Japan include LipiView II®, DR-1αTM, Keratograph 5M™, and idraTM. Goto et al. and Eom et al. reported significantly thinner LLT in MGD than in healthy eyes; Eom et al. also linked thinner LLT with greater gland dropout. Finis et al. reported that LLT ≤75 nm detected MGD with 65.8% sensitivity and 63.4% specificity. Arita et al. proposed pearl-like, Jupiter-like, and crystal-like patterns for healthy eyes, ADDE, and evaporative dry eye including MGD, respectively. Evidence for the LLT cutoff is limited, and only one interferometric-pattern classification is reported.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: The relevant studies were observational, with limited settings, differing diagnostic criteria and instruments, and insufficient consideration of regional or racial differences. Tear-volume and lipid-dynamic effects complicate LLT interpretation. Equipment is available in few facilities, is expensive, and sometimes images only the inferior cornea. No established interference-imaging criterion currently makes the technique beneficial for MGD diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Interference imaging may help assess lipid-layer impairment, but unresolved diagnostic questions require further research. Cost and difficulty of use have prompted attempts to construct more accessible devices.

document_sections.heading: CQ10 Is tear evaporation measurement useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Tear evaporation may reflect gland function, and many reports describe increased evaporation in oMGD versus healthy eyes. Because devices and testing conditions lack standardization and clinical use is uncommon, the guideline does not recommend the measurement for MGD diagnosis at present.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: The proposed link between tear lipids and evaporation remains partly speculative. Measurement commonly tracks humidity changes in a chamber around the eye and expresses evaporated water per surface area and time, often in g/cm2/sec. The review identified eight articles on oMGD; most compared patients with healthy controls and reported significantly higher evaporation. Goto et al. reported 5.8 ± 2.7x10-7g/cm2/ sec in oMGD versus 4.1 ± 1.4x10-7g/cm2/sec in healthy individuals (p = 0.0008). McCulley et al. found no significant increase when comparing dry eye with MGD against dry eye alone; humidity affected results, and MGD without dry eye was not assessed. McCann et al. reported 46.3 ± 22.9g/m2/hr in blepharitis versus 18.0 ± 10.7g/m2/hr in healthy controls (p < 0.001); a 32.3 g/m2/hr cutoff yielded 73% sensitivity and 86% specificity. Khanal et al. found differences between ADDE and evaporative dry eye, but considerable overlap gave only 77% sensitivity and 55% specificity.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Differences in MGD definitions, assessment methods, evaporation equipment, units, and unknown diagnostic cutoffs limit comparison. Evaporation in ADDE is not consistently characterized, so a measurement cannot be taken as exclusively reflecting gland function.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Evaporation measurement is noninvasive and might eventually inform oMGD diagnosis, severity, or treatment response. Wider equipment availability and studies defining cutoffs for MGD and related disorders are needed.

document_sections.heading: CQ11 Is IVCM useful in diagnosing MGD?
document_sections.content: IVCM can depict tissue at cellular resolution and has reportedly shown MGD-associated findings, but supporting studies are observational. Whether structures labelled as gland acini are actually acini must be verified. Contact with the epithelium and lengthy examinations impose patient burdens. The guideline cannot currently determine whether to recommend IVCM.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Early tear-lipid-layer IVCM images were too coarse to define features. Later equipment, including HRT II RCM, enabled cellular-level ocular imaging in specialized clinics. Reported assessments include presumed acinar density and dimensions, inflammatory cells, eyelid epithelium, gland orifices, and tissue reflectivity; Table 17 lists findings attributed to MGD. Matsumoto et al. reported significantly lower presumed acinar density and larger diameters than in normal eyes, associated with reduced lipid expression. Ibrahim et al. related confocal findings to tear tests, staining, secretion, dropout, and evaporation. For proposed cutoffs of 70 glands/mm2, 65 μm, 25 μm, and 300 cells /mm2, the respective sensitivity and specificity pairs were 81% and 81%, 90% and 81%, 86% and 96%, and 100% and 100%. Villani et al. additionally described enlarged orifices and altered reflectivity, proposing obstruction-related increased meibum viscosity as a possible explanation. Other reports relate more severe symptoms or disease to altered presumed acinar measurements, fibrosis, immune-cell findings, and corneal nerves; these associations need verification.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Zhou et al. argued that an oval structure labelled an acinus in upper-eyelid HRT II RCM images corresponds instead to a dermal–epidermal structure. They placed actual acini at 300 μm or deeper, beyond the instrument’s observation depth of up to 100 μm, and found a substantial discrepancy in measured cross-sectional area. Compression during examination means acinar visibility cannot be ruled out absolutely. High cost and required technical expertise also restrict routine use.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Research should examine upper-versus-lower eyelid histology and relationships with symptoms and surface findings. The identity of imaged structures needs independent confirmation: HRT II RCM records reflected light at 670 nm, and current imaging depth does not cover the entire gland. A deeper-reaching near-infrared device is proposed.

document_sections.heading: CQ12 Is measuring tear film osmolality useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Tear osmolality might reflect lipid-layer function, but diagnostic studies conflict. The guideline does not discourage this minimally invasive test while judging its current clinical relevance limited.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Osmolality is used as a dry-eye sign, although reproducibility has been questioned. MGD-associated evaporation might raise it. TearLabⓇ Osmolality System made small-sample measurements more accessible. Rico-Del-Viejo et al. reported increased osmolality when meibographic gland loss exceeded 50%. Xiao et al. found higher values in low-delivery than high-delivery MGD groups. One reported 308 mOsm/L cutoff had 68.6% sensitivity and 55.2% specificity. In contrast, Giannaccare et al. found no significant difference between symptomatic MGD and matched controls; Adil et al. found no association with dropout, and Randon et al. found no significant association with stage. TearLab ® testing costs about US$10 per eye, lacks JHI coverage, and is not widely used in Japan.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Conflicting results preclude a diagnostic recommendation. Inconsistent MGD recruitment criteria and possible selection bias contribute to uncertainty.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Osmolality can reflect both reduced tear turnover and increased evaporation, so it cannot isolate the lipid layer’s evaporation-related function. Barna et al. reported increased osmolality with reduced tear clearance in MGD. Better equipment might improve future usefulness.

document_sections.heading: CQ13 Is lipid quantification on eyelid margins useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Measuring eyelid-margin lipids is relevant to MGD biology, but its diagnostic usefulness cannot yet be determined. The test causes little patient disadvantage and permits relatively reproducible semiquantitation; without an established cutoff, however, it currently offers little diagnostic benefit.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Meibometry measures eyelid-margin lipids using devices including MeibometerⓇ MB550 and MB560. Yokoi et al. reported lower resting lipid levels in MGD than in controls and a tendency toward higher levels in ADDE; sampling and analysis refinements aimed to avoid compression-related overestimation. Komuro et al. reported lower levels in oMGD but higher levels in seborrheic MGD. Ashraf et al., using different methods, reported levels twice as high in MGD as in controls. Sampling, measurement, unmatched participant age and sex, menstrual cycle, and eyelid temperature may influence results. Few small observational studies have directly compared MGD with controls.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: The available studies were unmasked, old, and inconsistent; one had significant selection bias. MeibometerⓇ testing lacks JHI coverage and broad availability. Although relatively reproducible and noninvasive, it has no specified MGD cutoff.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Large studies using consistent methods could establish age- and sex-specific cutoffs. Simultaneous analysis of secretion components might also increase the device’s usefulness.

document_sections.heading: CQ14 Is a biochemical analysis of the meibomian gland secretions useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Biochemical studies have identified possible changes in meibum, but no MGD-specific marker or validated analysis method. Such analysis is not useful for current diagnosis and carries time, cost, access, and sampling burdens. Continued research may clarify MGD pathophysiology and support future treatments.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Meibum contains numerous polar and non-polar lipid components. Studies have used different methods to investigate composition and structure. Borchman et al. reported lower cholesterol ester/wax ester ratios and cholesterol ester quantities in MGD, but age-related findings complicate interpretation. Arita et al. reported unsaturated fatty acids in white and yellow meibum; other work associated linoleic acid with vascularity and plugging, though free fatty acids form only a small fraction of meibum. Shine et al. and Borchman et al. reported differing fatty-acid patterns, while Joffre et al. reported results contradicting earlier saturated-fatty-acid findings. Reports concerning branched hydrocarbons likewise disagree across methods. Investigations of phospholipids, sphingolipids, triglycerides, carotenoid-like components, and protein-like substances describe further possible differences. Studies using comparable methods are scarce and often small; no specific diagnostic marker has emerged.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Comparative studies were cross-sectional and used different MGD definitions, patient-selection methods, lipid components, and laboratory techniques. Findings for unsaturated fatty acids and branched hydrocarbons were inconsistent across facilities. Lipid analysis requires specialist facilities, substantial time and expense, and relatively large samples obtained by strong eyelid compression, which can cause marked discomfort.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Identifying components responsible for altered meibum properties could improve understanding and treatment development. Future MGD-specific markers and clinically practical testing kits might simplify diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: CQ15 Is measuring inflammatory biomarkers in tears useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Tear inflammatory-biomarker measurement is not currently useful for MGD diagnosis, although it might eventually support an adjunctive approach.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Seven studies assessed tear inflammatory biomarkers. Two examined individual candidates, Acidic Mammalian Chitinase and IL-17; the others investigated multiple markers, including TNF-α, IFN-γ, EGF, Lactoferrin, MMP-9, MIP-1α, RANTES, and several IL markers. Table 18 summarizes comparisons across MGD, dry eye, SS, and healthy groups. Results differ by biomarker and comparator. For example, TNF-α findings range from no significant difference to increases that also occur in dry eye without MGD; SS may show a greater increase than MGD. No individual marker has consistently distinguished MGD from both healthy eyes and dry eye. Musumeci et al. reported higher tear Acidic Mammalian Chitinase in MGD than in SS and controls, but that finding comes from one report and related IL-13 findings do not confirm it. Tear lipid analyses have also suggested possible differentiation among MGD, dry eye, and normal eyes, but evidence remains limited.

document_sections.heading: Problems and Biases
document_sections.content: Few reports evaluate MGD-specific tear biomarkers; comparator diseases differ, study populations are small, and publication bias may affect single-marker reports. The evidence is insufficient for diagnostic use.

document_sections.heading: Future Challenges and Trends
document_sections.content: Further studies should investigate relationships with MGD severity, diagnostic cutoffs, and possible marker combinations. Lipidomic approaches also need more evidence.

document_sections.heading: CQ16 Are bacteriological tests useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Neither bacterial culture nor polymerase-chain-reaction-based genomic testing has produced findings characteristic of MGD. Bacteriological tests are therefore not currently useful for its diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Explanation
document_sections.content: Bacteriological testing has an established history in blepharitis and rosacea, conditions whose clinical concepts partly overlap with MGD. The guideline identified seven studies that combined bacteriological tests with MGD diagnosis and specified diagnostic criteria. Their approaches fall broadly into culture and genomic sequencing; the sampled ocular sites differ.

document_sections.heading: CQ16 Are bacteriological tests useful in the diagnosis of MGD?
document_sections.content: Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus was frequently detected with and without MGD, so culture did not identify an organism specific to MGD. Some studies reported differences for Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa: one found that Staphylococcus aureus positivity fell as MGD became more severe, and another found lower Pseudomonas aeruginosa positivity in MGD. Other studies did not confirm these differences. Table 19 presents culture findings by sample, method and study group. Genomic sequencing examines ocular bacterial communities; 16S rRNA metagenomic analysis amplifies part of the 16S rRNA gene by polymerase chain reaction and is more commonly used than whole-genome metagenomics because of cost. Li et al. found no significant difference in overall community composition by MGD status. Dong et al. found no significant compositional difference between non-MGD and mild or moderate MGD, but did find one for severe MGD. Their studies identified different organisms through linear discrimination analysis, so the findings were inconsistent; Table 20 summarizes their comparisons and sampling sites. Another sequencing study suggested that Demodex may affect ocular bacterial communities. Sampling locations and test methods differed across studies, preventing straightforward comparison. Culture cannot detect every organism in a specimen, whereas sequencing describes community composition without accurately measuring bacterial counts. Neither method has established a bacterium, community pattern or positivity threshold characteristic of MGD. More evidence is needed to determine whether particular bacteria are directly involved; reports have also described newly identified bacteria in meibum.

document_sections.heading: Q17 What are the frequency and characteristics of keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders in MGD and what are the appropriate staining methods?
document_sections.content: Keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders are reported more often in MGD than in normal eyes and are considered milder than in ADDE. Whether they arise from associated dry eye or meibomian gland abnormalities remains disputed. No systematic analysis establishes their characteristic distribution in MGD, and studies disagree about whether epithelial injury tracks MGD severity, gland dropout, symptoms, eyelid vascularity or meibum expressibility. Shimazaki et al. observed greater injury when both gland dropout and orifice obstruction occurred, but no significant relationship when either finding occurred alone. Ibrahim et al. associated greater epithelial injury with higher inflammatory-cell density and acinar diameters and lower acinar-unit density. Fluorescein is the most versatile stain; Rose Bengal and lissamine green are also used. Ocular-surface assessment is not internationally standardized. Japanese studies scored fluorescein staining in three corneal regions at 0–3 points each, total 9 points, and Rose Bengal staining in three conjunctival/corneal regions at 0–3 points each, total 9 points. Studies in Europe and the United States used different corneal and conjunctival regions. Research restricted to MGD without dry eye is needed to clarify MGD's independent contribution.

document_sections.heading: CQ18 Is eyelid warming effective?
document_sections.content: Eyelid warming improves subjective MGD symptoms and meibum grade. The formal strength is Strongly recommend “implementation”; evidence is A (strong): Strongly confident in estimate of effect. The vote was 12/12 (100%) for that category. Reviews of 42 outcome-assessable articles found frequent improvements in symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT and epithelial disorders; many MGD studies enrolled approximately 30 patients, limiting certainty. The focused review selected six studies—three RCTs and three observational studies—using MGDRx, Eyebag, Blephasteam, Eye mask or Azuki no chikara. All reported symptom and meibum improvement; Arita et al. found significant meibum-grade improvement one month after treatment. Devices appeared more effective than towels and cost from a few US dollars to tens of dollars; they were reusable. JHI does not cover warming for MGD, although it is generally home care. Among 33 studies assessing symptoms, 32 reported improvement and 1 no change. Corresponding improvement/no-change counts were 13/5 among 18 studies for orifice and surrounding findings, 19/1 among 20 for meibum grade, 25/8 among 33 for BUT, and 10/5 among 15 for epithelial disorders. Among 10 studies assessing adverse events, 1 reported an event and 9 reported none; the reported event was temporary and reversible. The focused studies reported symptom improvement within 1 day, 2 weeks, 3 weeks or 4 weeks, depending on the study, and consistent improvement in meibum properties. Patient satisfaction was not directly studied, although one study recorded favorable comfort responses.

document_sections.heading: CQ19 Is eyelid hygiene effective?
document_sections.content: For MGD, cleaning with water-moistened cotton balls may improve symptoms and BUT; commercial cleansing agents may improve symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT and ocular-surface epithelial injury. Mild, non-serious adverse effects vary by cleanser and warrant caution. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation”; evidence is C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effects. Voting was 2/11 (18%) for strong implementation and 9/11 (82%) for marginal implementation; a member with COI did not vote. Evidence comprised one RCT comparing a new cleanser with a conventional cleanser and three observational studies, rather than a trial establishing the effect of hygiene itself. Methods, cleansing frequency and rinsing differed; cleanser-related COI bias could not be excluded. Assessments occurred after 3 months in the RCT, after 1 month and 8 weeks in cleanser studies, and after 6 weeks in the water study. All four studies found significant symptom improvement. Cleansers improved assessed orifice findings and meibum quality or expressibility; water cleaning did not significantly improve orifice findings but did improve BUT. Cleanser studies had mixed results for epithelial damage. The RCT recorded irritation in 21 of 40 eyes (52.5%) treated with a tea tree oil cleanser and 12 of 40 eyes (30%) treated with the conventional cleanser; two observational studies reported no adverse events. In one study, 22 patients without gland atrophy improved in vascularity, meibum quality and BUT after cleanser treatment, whereas six with atrophy did not show comparable improvement. Different baseline gland morphology may therefore influence response.

document_sections.heading: CQ20 Is meibomian gland expression effective?
document_sections.content: MGX is recommended as an option for oMGD because it improves subjective symptoms. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation”; evidence is C (weak): Limited confidence in estimated effect. Voting was 1/12 (8%) for strong and 11/12 (92%) for marginal implementation. The review included three RCTs, three prospective studies and one retrospective study, all concerning oMGD. Expression methods, accompanying care and follow-up differed. MGX alone improved OSDI or SPEED symptoms without consistently improving meibum, BUT, Schirmer values or corneal staining; compression-related pain burdens patients despite the absence of reported serious events. MGX lacks JHI coverage. Kaiserman et al. used monthly swab expression plus artificial tears four times a day: OSDI improved at 1 month and 2 months, but objective measures did not. Aketa et al. added MGX to twice-daily warming and hygiene, 1.5% levofloxacin four times a day, 0.1% fluorometholone three times a day, 0.1% hyaluronic acid four times a day and oral minocycline 100 mg twice a day; symptoms improved in both groups, with additional objective improvement including BUT after one month in the MGX group. Wang et al. added forceps expression to warming three times a day, hygiene, 0.3% tobramycin/0.1 dexamethasone once a day and 0.1% hyaluronic acid four times a day; at 1 month, additional objective findings improved. Other combined-treatment studies also reported improvements that cannot be assigned to MGX alone. Arita et al. found no improvement after eight expression sessions at 3-week intervals when assessed at 24 and 32 weeks; their separate combined-warming study reported improvement over 3 months in mild and moderate, but not severe, MGD. Study bias and differing regimens limit interpretation.

document_sections.heading: CQ21 Are diquafosol eye drops effective?
document_sections.content: DQS efficacy in MGD without dry eye is unknown. In concurrent MGD and dry eye, drops may improve symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, meibum grade, BUT and epithelial damage. Because JHI does not cover DQS for MGD alone, the formal strength is Marginally recommend “not to be implemented”; evidence is C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effect. Voting was 1/4 (25%) for marginal implementation and 3/4 (75%) against it, with eight COI exclusions. One RCT and three clinical studies all enrolled patients with dry eye. A Japanese epidemiological study reported MGD prevalence of 32.9%, dry-eye prevalence of 33.4%, and concurrent prevalence of 12.9%; MGD without dry eye was 20%, about 1.6 times the concurrent group. Evidence on MGD-specific objective effects comes from two small observational studies, and all reviewed studies were Japanese. The RCT compared a single DQS drop with an artificial-tear drop for up to 90 minutes. Other studies used DQS six times a day for 3 months, four times a day for ≥4 months (4–16 months), or for 2 months. Symptom results across longer studies differed. Plugging and vascularity improved at 1, 2, and 3 months in one study without significant change in margin irregularity or MCJ displacement; another reported improved composite margin scores after ≥4 months (4–16 months). Two studies found improved meibum grade at 3 months and 4–16 months. NIBUT improved up to 90 minutes in the RCT; longer studies reported BUT and epithelial-score improvements at their respective follow-ups. The RCT observed LLT improvement up to 60 minutes relative to artificial tears, and another study recorded increased LLT 20 minutes after instillation. Two studies reported later meibography improvements. One study stopped drops after eye pain in 1 out of 14 cases (7.1%); another reported irritation, tearing and discharge in 2 out of 32 cases (6.3%). No serious events were reported.

document_sections.heading: CQ22 Are antimicrobial eye drops effective?
