document_sections.content: Among antimicrobial drops, azithromycin had the supporting evidence. For MGD it improves symptoms, orifice and surrounding findings, and meibum grade; BUT benefit is weak and epithelial benefit limited. Adverse events are relatively frequent but generally mild. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation”; evidence is B (medium): Moderately confident in estimate of effect. Voting was 4/4 (100%) for marginal implementation, with eight COI exclusions. Four RCTs and three observational studies informed the review, including studies of posterior or chronic blepharitis. Studied concentrations were 1.0% and 1.5%, with variable schedules, duration and accompanying care. No other antimicrobial-drop literature met the specified evidence threshold. Studies reported symptom and margin improvements; fewer established meibum or epithelial effects, and COI-related bias could affect results. JHI covers azithromycin drops for conjunctivitis, blepharitis, hordeolum and dacryocystitis, including MGD with blepharitis. The document attributes bacteriostatic inhibition of eyelid bacterial lipase, anti-inflammatory activity and promotion of meibomian epithelial lipid secretion to azithromycin. Its viscosity can cause eye irritation and blurred vision; serious events were considered unlikely.

document_sections.heading: CQ23 Are ophthalmic ointments (excluding corticosteroid-based ophthalmic ointment)/ oily eye drops effective?
document_sections.content: Some ophthalmic ointments and lipid-containing drops reportedly improve MGD symptoms and examined clinical findings, but few products of each kind have been studied. The formal strength is Unable to make a clear recommendation.; evidence is D (very weak): Little confidence in estimate of effect. Voting was 1/4 (25%) for marginal implementation, 1/4 (25%) against it and 2/4 (50%) undecided, with eight COI exclusions. Three ointment studies examined an antimicrobial, an immunosuppressant and vitamin D3; only the immunosuppressant study was an RCT. Ofloxacin ointment improved tear-film stability and lid/orifice findings and has JHI coverage when blepharitis coexists. Vitamin D3 was reported to suppress keratinization and inflammation. The immunosuppressant ointment lacked MGD coverage and was associated with burning. Six lipid-drop studies included two RCTs; products contained castor oil, polar lipids, perfluorohexyl octane or mineral oil. Castor oil was described as having anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity; polar-lipid drops were reported to improve tear-film stability. Studies reported improvements in symptoms and various objective findings, with few non-serious adverse events, but evidence for each formulation remained limited. Castor oil needs preparation and cold storage; ready-made products were sold overseas and lacked JHI coverage for MGD. The review therefore did not make a clear recommendation for either product group.

document_sections.heading: CQ24 Is topical corticosteroid administration (eye drops and ointments) effective?
document_sections.content: Corticosteroid drops combined with warming and hygiene may improve MGD symptoms, BUT, eyelid-margin findings and meibum quality. Evidence is limited, and JHI covers use with concomitant blepharitis but not MGD alone. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation”; evidence is C (weak): Limited confidence in estimate of effect. Voting was 4/4 (100%) for marginal implementation, with eight COI exclusions. Two RCTs were reviewed; no qualifying corticosteroid-ointment study was found. Lee et al. compared 0.5% loteprednol etabonate plus twice-daily warming and hygiene in 30 patients against warming and hygiene in 30 patients over 2 months. At 1 month and 2 months, BUT, fluorescein staining, margin findings and meibum quality improved more with the drops. After one month, IL-6, IL-8 and IL-1b decreased in the drops group, whereas IL-6 and IL-8 decreased with warming and hygiene alone. No serious events or significant between-group difference in intraocular-pressure increase occurred; the formulation could not be prescribed in Japan. Akyol-Salman et al. compared betamethasone 0.1%-sulfacetamide sodium 10% plus hygiene in 10 patients with N-acetyl-cysteine plus hygiene in 10 patients. At 1 month, both groups improved BUT and Schirmer values versus baseline (P≤0.001), and burning, itching and blurred vision improved versus 1 day. Between-group improvement did not significantly differ for symptoms, BUT (P=0.232) or Schirmer values (P=0.202). No serious adverse events or increased intraocular pressure were reported. Because both groups received hygiene and one regimen combined corticosteroid with antibiotic, treatment-specific effects remain uncertain.

document_sections.heading: CQ25 Are cyclosporin A eye drops effective?
document_sections.content: CsA drops have shown limited improvements in MGD symptoms, eyelid findings and meibum properties. They are not considered an evidence-based MGD treatment and lack JHI coverage. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “not to be implemented”; evidence is D (very weak): Little confidence in estimate of effects. Voting was 4/4 (100%) against implementation, with eight COI exclusions. The review included three RCTs and two other studies; all used 0.05% CsA, outcomes differed and no CsA-related side effects were reported. Perry et al. compared 12 CsA-treated eyes with 14 artificial-tear-treated eyes: lid injection and vascularity and corneal injury improved, but symptoms and BUT did not. Schechter et al. studied ocular rosacea in 21 CsA eyes versus 16 artificial-tear eyes and reported improvements in Schirmer values, epithelial injury and symptoms; participants were exclusively Caucasian. Prabhasawat et al. studied MGD with BUT ≤ 8 seconds, comparing 36 CsA eyes with 34 artificial-tear eyes. BUT improved more with CsA, and meibum expressibility improved only after 1 month; symptoms, margin inflammation and epithelial injury did not differ. Both groups also received eyelid care, complicating attribution. A retrospective comparison of CsA plus hyaluronic acid against hyaluronic acid alone reported improvements in BUT, Schirmer values, vascularity and symptoms, but lacked masking. In a 12-week posterior-blepharitis study of 30 eyes, with 15 per group, CsA outperformed tobramycin and dexamethasone drops for several tear and eyelid findings; the small sample limited confidence.

document_sections.heading: CQ26 Is oral n-3 fatty acid administration effective?
document_sections.content: Oral n-3 (omega-3) fatty acids may improve MGD symptoms, eyelid-margin vascularity and BUT. Appropriate candidates, dose, formulation and interactions with usual diet remain uncertain. In Japan these formulations are supplements without JHI coverage for MGD. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation”; the evidence designation is C (weak): Little confidence in estimate of effect. Voting was 10/12 (83%) for marginal implementation and 2/12 (17%) against it. Six RCTs used 1.0–3.3 g/day for 3 months in five studies and 1 year in another. Formulations and concomitant treatment varied; five studies included EPA and DHA in differing ratios, two included vitamins A, C and E with DPA, and another included ALA, n-6 and n-9. One RCT assessed habitual dietary n-3 intake. Separate epidemiological studies reported average daily n-3 intakes of 1.87 g in a United States MGD group and 2.5 g in a Japanese oMGD group; none of the reviewed RCTs was Japanese. Three RCTs found greater OSDI improvement than controls at 3 months to 1 year; another found within-group OSDI improvement at 1 and 3 months without between-group comparison, and another found improved health-related quality of life after 3 months. Two RCTs found improved vascularity at 3 months and 1 year. Meibum findings were mixed, so improvement in meibum remains uncertain. Four studies found greater BUT improvement than controls at 1 month or 3 months; the 1-year study found improvement in both groups without a significant between-group difference. Epithelial findings were inconsistent. Two biochemical studies found increased serum n-3 (Omega 3) index, with additional red-cell and serum-ratio changes, but one found no meibum fatty-acid compositional change. One study found lower tear osmolality at 6 and 12 weeks. One RCT found no significant MGD-stage improvement in either group. Digestive upset occurred in two out of 64 patients (3.12%) in one study within 1 month and resolved after stopping treatment; another reported fish-tasting regurgitation leading two out of 64 patients (3.12%) to stop. No serious adverse events were observed.

document_sections.heading: CQ27 Is oral antimicrobial medication effective?
document_sections.content: The guideline separately assesses oral azithromycin and oral doxycycline or minocycline for MGD. Both recommendation groups received Marginally recommend “implementation”, with a 12/12 (100%) marginal-implementation vote. Evidence is B (medium): Moderately confident in estimated effect for oral azithromycin and C (weak): Little confidence in estimated effect for doxycycline and minocycline. Tetracycline was not assigned a recommendation strength or evidence grade because only one relevant article was available. Reviewed studies included MGD and related rosacea, posterior blepharitis or meibomitis; evidence for clarithromycin did not meet the stated threshold. Antimicrobial selection must account for adverse events, longer administration of tetracyclines and lack of JHI coverage for MGD. The document states that administration is contraindicated with renal or liver damage, in infants and children, and during pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: 1. Oral macrolide (azithromycin)
document_sections.content: Oral azithromycin improves subjective symptoms and meibomian orifice and surrounding findings in MGD. Its effect on meibum grade is unknown; effects on BUT and epithelial disorders are limited. Adverse events were infrequent and generally mild but require attention. Reviewed studies included five interventional studies and one observational study for several outcomes. Azithromycin was reported to act bacteriostatically, inhibit bacterial lipase, reduce inflammation and promote meibomian epithelial lipid secretion. Its shorter administration period was judged to confer comparatively fewer adverse effects than other oral antimicrobials, although cardiovascular effects warrant caution in patients with cardiovascular disorders. It lacks JHI coverage for ocular disease.

document_sections.heading: 2. Oral tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline, and tetracycline)
document_sections.content: Doxycycline and minocycline improve MGD symptoms; the symptomatic effect of tetracycline is unknown. Improvement in orifice and surrounding findings is considered likely, meibum-grade effects remain unclear and BUT effects are limited overall. Doxycycline adverse events were relatively frequent, particularly digestive effects, and longer tetracycline-class treatment calls for caution. JHI covers some ocular indications but not MGD. The document identifies bacteriostatic, bacterial-lipase-inhibitory and anti-inflammatory actions for this antimicrobial group. It distinguishes the evidence for individual drugs in the following subsections.

document_sections.heading: 1) Doxycycline
document_sections.content: Seven interventional studies and one observational study assessed symptoms and supported oral doxycycline for MGD and related posterior blepharitis or ocular rosacea. Six interventional studies and one observational study assessed orifice and surrounding findings and found improvement. Meibum-grade effects remain unknown because high-level evidence was unavailable. BUT prolongation was limited overall, despite improvement in some studies. Six interventional studies reported epithelial improvement. Seven interventional studies assessed adverse events, which were relatively frequent and warrant caution. The guideline judges doxycycline therapeutically effective and marginally recommends its implementation. Compared with azithromycin, its longer treatment duration was considered less favorable for safety and benefit relative to cost. JHI covers doxycycline for eyelid abscess, dacryocystitis, hordeolum and keratitis, but not MGD.

document_sections.heading: 2) Minocycline
document_sections.content: One RCT suggested improvement in MGD symptoms. One RCT and two observational studies reported improvement in orifice and surrounding findings in MGD or meibomitis. Meibum-grade effects remain unclear. One RCT and one observational study found longer BUT, while epithelial improvement was limited or absent. An RCT reported infrequent digestive symptoms requiring caution. The guideline judges oral minocycline therapeutically useful and marginally recommends implementation. It describes bacteriostatic, bacterial-lipase-inhibitory and anti-inflammatory actions. Use should be avoided in infants, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and patients with liver or kidney disease. JHI covers dacryocystitis and hordeolum, not MGD.

document_sections.heading: 3) Tetracycline
document_sections.content: High-level evidence does not establish oral tetracycline's effects on MGD symptoms, meibum grade, epithelial disorders or adverse events. One RCT reported improved orifice and surrounding findings and possible BUT prolongation in rosacea. The guideline considers therapeutic benefit for MGD unlikely on the available evidence and notes that azithromycin, doxycycline and minocycline are now more commonly used. Because only one MGD article was available, tetracycline was excluded from recommendation-strength and evidence-strength assessment.

document_sections.heading: CQ28 Is intense pulsed light effective?
document_sections.content: IPL improves MGD symptoms, meibomian orifice and lid-margin findings, meibum grade, BUT and epithelial disorders. Reported adverse events were infrequent, mild and reversible. Although the evidence-based appraisal strongly favored treatment, the formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation” because IPL was not approved for MGD in Japan as of November 2022 and lacked JHI coverage. Evidence is A (strong): Strongly confident in estimate of effect; voting was 8/8 (100%) for marginal implementation, with four COI exclusions. The review included seven RCTs. Four of five symptom-assessing studies reported improvement, as did both studies assessing margin findings, five assessing meibum grade, four assessing BUT, and three of four assessing epithelial disorders. One RCT reported pain, heat sensation and partial eyelash loss. All seven RCTs treated lower eyelids only; four also performed meibum expression. Application numbers were three, five or eight, at schedules including every 3 weeks, every 4 weeks, or days 1, 15, and 45. Follow-up extended to 6 months, 8 months or 9 months, without established time to recurrence or response duration. No internationally agreed protocol establishes application frequency, number or device energy, and the contribution of concurrent expression remains untested. In Japan, treatment cost was approximately 5,000 to 15,000 yen/ treatment without insurance. Studies reported reduced tear IL-6, IL-17 and PG-E after IPL; meibum liquefaction through deeper skin warming was also proposed. Long-term safety for the lens and retina has not been confirmed.

document_sections.heading: CQ29 Is thermal pulsation therapy effective?
document_sections.content: Thermal pulsation improves MGD symptoms and some orifice and surrounding findings, meibum quality and BUT. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “implementation” because JHI does not cover it; evidence is B (medium): Moderately confident in estimate of effect. Voting was 6/6 (100%) for marginal implementation, with six COI exclusions. Eight RCTs assessed LipiFlow®; each administered one 12-minute treatment. Five studies compared warming, one examined use before cataract surgery, one compared oral antimicrobials and one compared integrin-antagonist drops. Across the eight studies, four reported improved symptoms. Plugging improved in two out of four studies, meibum quality in three out of five, BUT in two out of seven, and corneal epithelial injury in one out of five. Six assessed adverse events: two reported none and four reported mild events, predominantly immediate discomfort; no serious events occurred. Control regimens and MGD severity varied, limiting consistency. Detailed warming comparisons found symptom improvement after LipiFlow® in all five studies, with mixed between-group objective differences. The cataract-surgery study included healthy individuals as well as patients with MGD. Another comparison favored integrin-antagonist drops for symptoms and eyelid vascularity. LipiFlow® was approved as a Japanese medical device in 2019 but remained outside JHI coverage as of 2021. Studies suggest greater suitability when changes in meibum quality and gland morphology are mild and disease duration is short.

document_sections.heading: CQ30 Is probing effective?
document_sections.content: Intraductal probing may improve subjective symptoms in oMGD, but provides little improvement in obstruction-related findings, meibum grade, BUT or keratoconjunctival epithelial disorders. It is invasive, may require repetition and lacks JHI coverage. The formal strength is Marginally recommend “not to be implemented”; evidence is D (very weak): Little confidence in estimate of effect. Voting was 12/12 (100%) against implementation. Two controlled reports combined probing with other care, preventing a reliable estimate of probing alone; three additional non-RCT studies were considered. Kheirkhah et al. compared probing followed by antibiotic/corticosteroid ointment, probing followed by lubricant ointment, and lubricant ointment without probing. Both probed groups improved symptoms at 1 month, but BUT and other findings did not change; greater improvement with the anti-inflammatory ointment complicated attribution. Huang et al. compared IPL, probing and combined IPL/probing and reported the greatest improvement with combined care, without isolating probing's effect. Ma et al. compared probing plus 0.1% fluorometholone with 0.1% fluorometholone alone; both improved some findings. Incekalan et al. found no significant between-group difference in improvement ratios when probing was added to conventional care. Sik Sarman et al. reported improvement without an untreated control and with additional post-probing treatment. Eyelid or orifice bleeding can occur during probing; the reviewed studies did not require special measures to stop it or report subsequent complications.

document_sections.heading: Chapter 5
document_sections.content: After publication, the supervisory, preparation and systematic-review teams planned to disseminate and use the guideline while monitoring new evidence. A shortened version was under consideration. Publication and professional-society websites were identified as dissemination routes, and questionnaires through relevant societies were proposed to assess use. Revision was planned in five years and additionally when important evidence emerged.
